TOUR.G12.T1.PROIMAGE.A1.title: Professional image in the tourism industry
TOUR.G12.T1.PROIMAGE.A1.description: How the image of the company (name, logo, slogan, website, stationery, marketing material, product packaging, appearance of the business, environmental and customer-service policies) and the image of the staff (professional appearance, uniforms, dress code, personal hygiene, grooming, interaction with customers, communication skills) build a professional image.
TOUR.G12.T1.PROIMAGE.A1.recovery_strategy: Ask WHO the factor belongs to: the BUSINESS (logo, slogan, website, stationery, policies) = company image; the PERSON serving you (uniform, grooming, hygiene, communication) = staff image. Both together create the professional image.

questions.question: What is meant by a 'professional image' in the tourism industry?
options: The overall impression a business and its staff give to customers through how they look and behave
Only the price list a business charges its customers
The number of branches a company owns
How far a tourist has to travel to reach the business
questions.expected: The overall impression a business and its staff give to customers through how they look and behave
questions.memo: A professional image is the impression created by both the company (logo, look, policies) and its staff (appearance, behaviour, communication).

questions.question: Which of these is part of the COMPANY'S image rather than the staff's image?
options: A guide's friendly tone of voice
questions.memo: The logo and slogan belong to the business itself. Uniform, hygiene and tone of voice are part of the individual staff member's image.

questions.question: Which factor contributes to a professional STAFF image?
options: The design of the company website
The colour of the company stationery
questions.memo: Grooming and hygiene are about the individual employee, so they form part of the staff image. The website, stationery and packaging belong to the company image.

questions.question: True or false: A messy, rude employee can damage a tourism company's professional image even if the office looks smart.
questions.memo: Customers judge the business through the staff they meet. Poor staff conduct harms the image no matter how smart the premises are.

questions.question: Why is a smart, consistent uniform good for a tourism business's image?
options: It makes staff easy to identify and shows a neat, professional standard
It allows the business to pay staff less
It removes the need for any customer service
It increases the price tourists must pay
questions.expected: It makes staff easy to identify and shows a neat, professional standard
questions.memo: Uniforms make staff recognisable to customers and present a tidy, unified, professional look.

questions.question: A short, memorable phrase used to advertise a company, such as part of its image, is called a _________.
questions.memo: A slogan is a short catchy phrase that helps form the company's image and brand.

questions.question: Which of the following would BEST improve the professional image staff present to customers?
options: Training staff in good communication and a polite, helpful manner
Hiding from customers who ask questions
Allowing staff to wear any clothing they like at work
questions.expected: Training staff in good communication and a polite, helpful manner
questions.memo: Communication skills and a helpful attitude are central to a professional staff image and good customer interaction.

questions.question: Sort each factor under whether it is part of the COMPANY image or the STAFF image.
questions.memo: Company image = things owned by the business (logo, website, marketing). Staff image = things about the individual worker (uniform, grooming, communication).

questions.question: Which item below is part of a company's image through its written and printed materials?
options: A staff member's name badge worn on a shirt
questions.memo: Stationery and letterheads are produced by the company and carry its branding, so they form part of the company image.

questions.question: True or false: A company's environmental and customer-service policies form part of its professional image.
questions.memo: Policies on how a business treats the environment and its customers shape how the public sees the company, so they are part of its image.

questions.question: Good personal _________ — being clean and well presented — is an important part of a staff member's professional image.
questions.memo: Personal hygiene (cleanliness and neat presentation) is part of how an employee presents a professional image.

questions.question: How does a strong professional image benefit a tourism business?
options: It builds customer trust and attracts repeat business
It guarantees the business pays no tax
It removes the need to train staff
It makes the business invisible to competitors
questions.expected: It builds customer trust and attracts repeat business
questions.memo: A professional image gives customers confidence, which encourages them to return and to recommend the business.

questions.question: A tour operator has no uniform. Which factor then becomes most important for the staff's professional image?
options: The colour of the office walls
The brand of the company's computers
questions.memo: Where no uniform is worn, a clear dress code keeps staff looking neat and professional.

questions.question: True or false: Product packaging and the physical appearance of the business premises both contribute to the company's image.
questions.memo: How products are packaged and how the premises look both shape the impression customers form of the company.

questions.question: The way an employee speaks and listens to customers is part of their _________ skills, which shape the staff image.
questions.memo: Communication skills — speaking clearly and listening well — are key to the impression staff make on customers.

questions.question: Which of these is the BEST example of staff harming a company's professional image?
options: An untidy employee arguing loudly with a customer
An employee greeting a guest warmly
An employee wearing a clean uniform
An employee answering a question politely
questions.expected: An untidy employee arguing loudly with a customer
questions.memo: Untidy appearance combined with rude behaviour damages the impression customers form of the whole business.

questions.question: A consistent logo, colours and slogan used across all of a company's materials is known as its:
questions.memo: Branding is the consistent use of a logo, colours and slogan that make a company recognisable and shape its image.

questions.question: Sort each action under whether it strengthens or weakens a professional image.

items.text: Staff greet every guest by name

questions.memo: Neatness, helpfulness and clear materials strengthen the image; untidiness, rudeness and careless materials weaken it.

questions.question: Why should a tourism business keep its premises clean and well maintained?
options: A tidy, well-kept premises gives customers a good first impression
It allows the business to ignore its staff
It means the business never has to advertise
It lowers the quality of service expected
questions.expected: A tidy, well-kept premises gives customers a good first impression
questions.memo: The physical appearance of the premises is the first thing many customers notice and forms part of the company image.

questions.question: True or false: A professional image is built by the company and its staff working together, not by one alone.
questions.memo: Both the company image (branding, premises, policies) and the staff image (appearance, conduct, communication) must work together to create a professional image.

TOUR.G12.T1.CONDEMP.A1.title: Conditions of employment
TOUR.G12.T1.CONDEMP.A1.description: Basic conditions of employment in a chosen tourism field (airlines, hotels or national parks): working hours, leave, remuneration and deductions, overtime, the role of the Basic Conditions of Employment Act and the Department of Labour in protecting workers.
TOUR.G12.T1.CONDEMP.A1.recovery_strategy: Remember there is a legal floor: the Basic Conditions of Employment Act sets minimums (hours, leave, notice). An employer may offer more than the minimum but not less.

questions.question: What do 'conditions of employment' mean?
options: The terms under which a person works, such as hours, leave and pay
The weather on the day a person starts work
The number of customers a business serves
The brand of uniform a company chooses
questions.expected: The terms under which a person works, such as hours, leave and pay
questions.memo: Conditions of employment are the working terms — hours, leave, pay, deductions and similar — that apply to an employee's job.

questions.question: Which South African law sets the minimum conditions of employment?
options: The Basic Conditions of Employment Act
questions.expected: The Basic Conditions of Employment Act
questions.memo: The Basic Conditions of Employment Act, overseen by the Department of Labour, sets the legal minimum working conditions in South Africa.

questions.question: True or false: An employer may legally offer worse conditions than the minimum set by the Basic Conditions of Employment Act.
questions.memo: The Act sets a legal floor. An employer may offer more than the minimum but never less.

questions.question: Paid time off that a worker is entitled to each year is called annual _________.
questions.memo: Annual leave is the paid time off a worker may take each year, and is part of their conditions of employment.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of a condition of employment?
options: The number of working hours per week
The colour of the company logo
The brand of coffee in the staff room
How many tourists visited last year
questions.expected: The number of working hours per week
questions.memo: Working hours per week are a basic condition of employment set out in law and in the contract.

questions.question: Which government department is responsible for protecting workers' basic conditions of employment?
options: The Department of Labour (Employment and Labour)
questions.expected: The Department of Labour (Employment and Labour)
questions.memo: The Department of Employment and Labour oversees and enforces the Basic Conditions of Employment Act.

questions.question: True or false: Sick leave and maternity leave are types of leave covered by conditions of employment.
questions.memo: Annual leave, sick leave and maternity leave are all forms of leave set out in the basic conditions of employment.

questions.question: Sort each item under whether it ADDS to a worker's pay or is DEDUCTED from it.
questions.memo: Salary, overtime and allowances add to pay; tax, UIF and pension contributions are deducted from it.

questions.question: Extra pay earned for working beyond normal hours is called:
questions.memo: Overtime is the extra pay a worker earns for hours worked beyond the normal working day or week.

questions.question: Why are clear conditions of employment important for an employee in the tourism industry?
options: They protect the worker by setting out their rights, hours and pay
They allow the worker to ignore all instructions
They remove the need for the worker to come to work
They decide which tourists may visit the country
questions.expected: They protect the worker by setting out their rights, hours and pay
questions.memo: Clear conditions protect the worker by stating their rights and what they can expect regarding hours, pay and leave.

questions.question: Money taken off a worker's pay, such as tax or UIF, is known as a _________.
questions.memo: A deduction is money subtracted from gross pay, for example PAYE tax, UIF or pension contributions.

questions.question: A hotel requires staff to work shifts, including some weekends. This is an example of regulating which condition of employment?
options: The star grading of the hotel
questions.memo: Shift patterns and weekend work fall under the working-hours condition of employment.

questions.question: True or false: Conditions of employment differ from one tourism field to another, such as between an airline and a national park.
questions.memo: While the legal minimum applies to all, specific conditions (shifts, allowances, duties) vary between fields such as airlines, hotels and national parks.

questions.question: Which of the following is a benefit an employer might offer ABOVE the legal minimum conditions?
options: Extra paid leave days each year
Refusing to pay for overtime worked
Giving less than the minimum notice period
questions.expected: Extra paid leave days each year
questions.memo: Offering more leave than the legal minimum is a benefit above the basic conditions. The other options break the law.

questions.question: The money a worker is paid for their work is called their _________.
questions.memo: Remuneration is the payment (wage or salary) a worker receives for their work.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a basic condition of employment?
options: The tourist attractions a customer chooses to visit
Notice period when leaving a job
questions.expected: The tourist attractions a customer chooses to visit
questions.memo: Which attractions a tourist visits has nothing to do with employment terms. Notice, leave and working hours are all conditions of employment.

questions.question: UIF, deducted from a worker's pay, stands for:
questions.memo: UIF is the Unemployment Insurance Fund, a deduction that helps workers who lose their income.

questions.question: True or false: A worker is entitled to a fixed period of notice before their employment is ended.
questions.memo: A notice period before termination is a basic condition of employment protected by law.

questions.question: Sort each item under whether it is a CONDITION OF EMPLOYMENT or NOT a condition of employment.

items.text: The colour of the tour bus
The brand of the company's pens

questions.memo: Leave, hours, pay and notice are conditions of employment. The colour of a bus or brand of pens are not.

questions.question: Why does the law set minimum conditions of employment?
options: To protect workers from being treated unfairly
To stop tourists from visiting the country
To force all businesses to charge the same prices
To remove the need for any contracts
questions.expected: To protect workers from being treated unfairly
questions.memo: Minimum conditions exist to protect employees and ensure they are treated fairly regarding hours, pay and leave.

TOUR.G12.T1.CONTRACT.A1.title: Contract of employment
TOUR.G12.T1.CONTRACT.A1.description: The contract of employment as the written agreement describing basic conditions: working hours, uniform allowances, travel benefits, leave, core duties, fringe benefits, remuneration and deductions, termination of service, professional accountability and service ethics.
TOUR.G12.T1.CONTRACT.A1.recovery_strategy: A fringe benefit is something EXTRA the worker GETS (travel perks, uniform allowance); a deduction is money TAKEN OFF pay (tax, UIF, pension). Sort each item by whether it adds to or subtracts from the worker.

questions.question: What is a contract of employment?
options: A written agreement setting out the conditions under which an employee works
A list of tourist attractions in a province
A ticket for an international flight
A receipt for a hotel booking
questions.expected: A written agreement setting out the conditions under which an employee works
questions.memo: A contract of employment is the written agreement between employer and employee describing the basic conditions of the job.

questions.question: Which of these would you expect to find in a contract of employment?
options: A map of the world's time zones
A list of World Heritage Sites
questions.memo: A contract sets out the job terms such as hours, leave, duties and pay.

questions.question: True or false: A contract of employment is an agreement between the employer and the employee.
questions.memo: The contract is signed by both the employer and the employee and binds both to its terms.

questions.question: A travel benefit, such as discounted flights for airline staff, is an example of a fringe _________.
questions.memo: A fringe benefit is an extra perk a worker receives in addition to pay, such as discounted travel.

questions.question: Which of the following is a fringe BENEFIT rather than a deduction?
questions.memo: A uniform allowance is an extra the worker receives (a benefit). Tax, pension and UIF are taken off pay (deductions).

questions.question: The part of a contract that explains how and when the job may be ended is called:
questions.memo: Termination of service sets out the rules and notice for ending the employment.

questions.question: Sort each contract item under whether it is a BENEFIT to the worker or a DEDUCTION from pay.

items.text: Medical aid subsidy from the employer

questions.memo: Benefits are extras the worker GETS (travel perks, allowances, subsidies); deductions are amounts TAKEN OFF pay (tax, pension, UIF).

questions.question: The duties an employee is mainly employed to carry out are called their:
questions.memo: Core duties are the main tasks the employee is hired to perform, set out in the contract.

questions.question: True or false: A contract of employment lists the worker's salary and any deductions from it.
questions.memo: Remuneration (pay) and deductions are basic items described in a contract of employment.

questions.question: Why is it important for an employee to have a written contract of employment?
options: It records what both sides agreed, protecting employer and employee
It allows the employee to skip work whenever they like
It decides the exchange rate of the rand
It books the employee's holiday flights
questions.expected: It records what both sides agreed, protecting employer and employee
questions.memo: A written contract is proof of the agreed terms, protecting both parties if a dispute arises.

questions.question: The pay a worker receives for their work, as written in the contract, is called _________.
questions.memo: Remuneration is the wage or salary stated in the contract of employment.

questions.question: A contract states that staff must act honestly and put guests' interests first. This describes the employee's:
questions.memo: Professional accountability and service ethics describe the standard of honest, responsible behaviour expected of the employee.

questions.question: True or false: Once signed, a contract of employment is binding on both the employer and the employee.
questions.memo: A signed contract is legally binding, so both parties must keep to its agreed terms.

questions.question: Which item below would form part of the 'leave' section of a contract?
options: The number of paid holiday days per year
The price tourists pay for a tour
The exchange rate for US dollars
The location of an icon on a map
questions.expected: The number of paid holiday days per year
questions.memo: The leave section covers paid time off such as annual, sick and family leave.

questions.question: A clothing allowance given so staff can buy work clothing is an example of a fringe _________.
questions.memo: A uniform or clothing allowance is an extra the worker receives, so it is a fringe benefit.

questions.question: How does a contract of employment differ from a code of conduct?
options: A contract sets the terms (pay, hours, leave); a code of conduct guides behaviour
They are exactly the same document
A contract is only for tourists, a code only for staff
A contract decides which currency to use abroad
questions.expected: A contract sets the terms (pay, hours, leave); a code of conduct guides behaviour
questions.memo: The contract sets out the working terms; the code of conduct guides how staff should behave. They serve different purposes.

questions.question: Which of these is a DEDUCTION that would appear on a worker's payslip?
questions.memo: A pension contribution is money taken off pay, so it is a deduction. Benefits, allowances and bonuses add to pay.

questions.question: True or false: A contract of employment should describe the basic conditions agreed, such as hours, duties, leave and pay.
questions.memo: Describing the basic conditions — hours, duties, leave, pay and termination — is exactly what a contract of employment does.

questions.question: Sort each item under whether it is part of a CONTRACT of employment or NOT part of it.

items.text: The weather forecast for next week

questions.memo: Pay, duties, leave and termination terms all belong in a contract. The weather and a tourist's meal do not.

questions.question: What should an employee do before signing a contract of employment?
options: Read it carefully and make sure they understand and agree to all the terms
Sign it without reading to save time
Change the terms in pen after signing
Ignore the pay and leave sections
questions.expected: Read it carefully and make sure they understand and agree to all the terms
questions.memo: Because a signed contract is binding, the employee should read and understand all terms before agreeing.

TOUR.G12.T1.CODECON.A1.title: Purpose & value of a code of conduct
TOUR.G12.T1.CODECON.A1.description: A code of conduct for staff: its purpose (spells out expected conduct in performing duties and guides staff facing ethical challenges) and its value (creates a co-operative, collaborative atmosphere and promotes integrity in the workplace).
TOUR.G12.T1.CODECON.A1.recovery_strategy: A code of conduct is about BEHAVIOUR and ethics (how staff should act); a contract is about TERMS (pay, hours, leave). The code guides decisions; the contract sets the deal.

questions.question: What is a code of conduct in a tourism business?
options: A set of rules spelling out the behaviour expected of staff
A map of the country's borders
A list of currency exchange rates
questions.expected: A set of rules spelling out the behaviour expected of staff
questions.memo: A code of conduct sets out how staff are expected to behave when carrying out their duties.

questions.question: What is the main PURPOSE of a code of conduct?
options: To spell out expected conduct and guide staff facing ethical challenges
To set the exchange rate of the rand
To plan a tourist's day-by-day itinerary
To decide which vaccinations a tourist needs
questions.expected: To spell out expected conduct and guide staff facing ethical challenges
questions.memo: Its purpose is to make clear how staff should behave and to guide them when they face difficult, ethical decisions.

questions.question: What is a key VALUE of having a code of conduct in the workplace?
options: It creates a co-operative atmosphere and promotes integrity
It removes the need to pay staff
It lowers the cost of fuel
questions.expected: It creates a co-operative atmosphere and promotes integrity
questions.memo: A code of conduct builds a co-operative, collaborative atmosphere and encourages honest, ethical behaviour (integrity).

questions.question: True or false: A code of conduct only describes a worker's salary and leave.
questions.memo: Salary and leave belong in the contract. A code of conduct is about behaviour and ethics, not pay.

questions.question: Honest, fair and ethical behaviour promoted by a code of conduct is summed up in the word _________.
questions.memo: Integrity means acting honestly and ethically — a key value a code of conduct promotes.

questions.question: An employee is unsure whether to accept a large gift from a supplier. How does a code of conduct help?
options: It guides the employee on the right, ethical thing to do
It tells the employee the exchange rate
It books the employee a holiday
It decides the employee's working hours
questions.expected: It guides the employee on the right, ethical thing to do
questions.memo: A code of conduct guides staff through ethical challenges, such as whether accepting a gift is appropriate.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis by choosing the strong supporting points.
questions.thesis: A code of conduct is valuable for a tourism business.

pool.text: It guides staff to behave ethically and consistently
It builds a co-operative, trusting atmosphere among staff
It promotes integrity, which protects the company's reputation
It sets the daily exchange rate for foreign currency
It decides which attractions are World Heritage Sites

questions.memo: The strong points all link the code to ethical behaviour, teamwork and reputation. The red herrings are unrelated to a code of conduct.

questions.question: True or false: A code of conduct guides staff members who face ethical challenges in their work.
questions.memo: Guiding staff through ethical challenges is one of the main purposes of a code of conduct.

questions.question: Which of these behaviours would a tourism code of conduct most likely require?
options: Treating every customer with honesty and respect
Taking money from the till for personal use
questions.expected: Treating every customer with honesty and respect
questions.memo: A code of conduct sets standards such as honesty and respect towards customers.

questions.question: How does a code of conduct help create a better working atmosphere?
options: Everyone knows the standards expected, so staff co-operate and trust each other
It allows each worker to make up their own rules
It stops the business from serving tourists
It removes all managers from the workplace
questions.expected: Everyone knows the standards expected, so staff co-operate and trust each other
questions.memo: Shared, clear standards build co-operation and trust, improving the workplace atmosphere.

questions.question: A code of conduct mainly deals with staff _________ — how they should act at work.
questions.memo: A code of conduct is about behaviour — the standard of conduct expected of staff.

questions.question: Why is it useful to study examples of codes of conduct from different tourism businesses?
options: To see how different businesses set out the behaviour they expect
To find the cheapest flights to book
To locate icons on a world map
questions.expected: To see how different businesses set out the behaviour they expect
questions.memo: Comparing real codes shows how various businesses describe expected conduct and ethical standards.

questions.question: True or false: A code of conduct and a contract of employment are the same document with the same purpose.
questions.memo: They are different: the contract sets the terms of the job (pay, hours); the code of conduct sets standards of behaviour.

questions.question: Which of the following is an ethical workplace value promoted by a code of conduct?
questions.memo: Honesty is an ethical value a code of conduct promotes; the others are the opposite of what it encourages.

questions.question: A behaviour that goes against accepted ethical standards is described as _________.
questions.memo: Unethical behaviour breaks the ethical standards a code of conduct is meant to uphold.

questions.question: A tour guide is offered a bribe to give one shop preference. According to a code of conduct, the guide should:
options: Refuse the bribe and act honestly
Tell the customers to pay the bribe
questions.expected: Refuse the bribe and act honestly
questions.memo: A code of conduct requires honest, ethical behaviour, so the guide should refuse the bribe.

questions.question: Which statement about a code of conduct is TRUE?
options: It applies to all staff and sets a shared standard of behaviour
It only applies to the manager
It changes the exchange rate daily
It replaces the need for any training
questions.expected: It applies to all staff and sets a shared standard of behaviour
questions.memo: A code of conduct applies across the business, giving all staff one shared standard of behaviour.

questions.question: True or false: Promoting integrity in the workplace is one of the values of a code of conduct.
questions.memo: Promoting integrity — honest, ethical conduct — is a stated value of having a code of conduct.

questions.question: A code of conduct contributes to good customer service mainly because:
options: Staff behave consistently and professionally towards customers
It lowers the price of every tour
It removes the need for feedback
questions.expected: Staff behave consistently and professionally towards customers
questions.memo: When staff follow a code of conduct, they treat customers consistently and professionally, improving service.

questions.question: Which pairing of purpose and value of a code of conduct is correct?
options: Purpose: guide expected conduct — Value: builds integrity and co-operation
Purpose: set the rand exchange rate — Value: cheaper flights
Purpose: list World Heritage Sites — Value: faster customs
Purpose: choose the menu — Value: more vaccinations
questions.expected: Purpose: guide expected conduct — Value: builds integrity and co-operation
questions.memo: The purpose is to guide expected conduct and ethical decisions; the value is a co-operative atmosphere and integrity.

TOUR.G12.T1.TIMEZONES.A1.title: World time zones
TOUR.G12.T1.TIMEZONES.A1.description: Time-zone concepts (UTC, Greenwich, hemispheres, equator, standard time, local time, the international date line, the 24-hour clock, latitude and longitude); reading a world time-zone map; daylight saving time; simple calculations of arrival and departure times; and jet lag, its symptoms and how to ease it.
TOUR.G12.T1.TIMEZONES.A1.recovery_strategy: Travel EAST = clocks go FORWARD (add hours); travel WEST = clocks go BACK (subtract hours). UTC is the world reference time at Greenwich; add a place's offset to find its local time.

questions.question: What is a time zone?
options: A region of the world that shares the same standard time
A border crossing between two countries
questions.expected: A region of the world that shares the same standard time
questions.memo: A time zone is an area that keeps the same standard clock time, set relative to UTC.

questions.question: World time is measured from a reference line that passes through Greenwich, near London. This reference is called:
questions.memo: UTC, based on the Greenwich meridian, is the world reference time from which other zones are measured.

questions.question: When you travel EAST across time zones, the local clock time generally:
questions.memo: Travelling east, you move towards later local times, so clocks go forward.

questions.question: When you travel WEST across time zones, the local clock time generally:
questions.memo: Travelling west, you move towards earlier local times, so clocks go back.

questions.question: South Africa uses UTC+2. If it is 10:00 UTC, what is the standard time in South Africa?
questions.memo: Add the offset of +2 hours to UTC: 10:00 + 2 = 12:00 in South Africa.

questions.question: The imaginary line at roughly 180° longitude, where the date changes by one day, is the international _________ line.
questions.memo: The international date line, near 180° longitude, is where the calendar date changes from one day to the next.

questions.question: True or false: The 24-hour clock writes 3 o'clock in the afternoon as 15:00.
questions.memo: On the 24-hour clock, afternoon and evening hours continue from 13:00 to 23:59, so 3 p.m. is 15:00.

questions.question: What is daylight saving time (DST)?
options: Moving the clock forward in summer to make better use of daylight
A currency used only in summer
A rule that stops all travel at night
questions.expected: Moving the clock forward in summer to make better use of daylight
questions.memo: Daylight saving time shifts the clock forward in summer so people enjoy more daylight in the evening.

questions.question: A traveller arrives feeling tired and out of step after a long flight across several time zones. This is known as:
questions.memo: Jet lag is the tiredness and disturbed body clock caused by crossing several time zones quickly.

questions.question: Which is a good way to reduce the effects of jet lag?
options: Drink plenty of water and adjust to the new time zone's sleep pattern
Drink lots of strong coffee before sleeping
questions.expected: Drink plenty of water and adjust to the new time zone's sleep pattern
questions.memo: Staying hydrated and shifting to the new local sleeping times helps the body adjust and eases jet lag.

questions.question: The reference time used worldwide is based on the line of 0° longitude at _________.
questions.memo: The prime meridian (0° longitude) runs through Greenwich, near London, the basis of world time.

questions.question: A city to the WEST of South Africa is at UTC-3. If South Africa (UTC+2) shows 14:00, what is the time in that city?
questions.memo: The city is 5 hours behind South Africa (from +2 to -3). 14:00 minus 5 hours = 09:00.

questions.question: True or false: When planning international flights, time zones must be considered so arrival times are correct in local time.
questions.memo: Crossing time zones changes local arrival and departure times, so they must be taken into account when planning travel.

questions.question: Lines that run from east to west and measure how far north or south of the equator a place is are called lines of:
questions.memo: Lines of latitude run east-west and measure distance north or south of the equator.

questions.question: Place these stages of a long-haul journey in the correct ORDER from first to last.

items.text: Check in and board the flight at the departure airport
Adjust your watch to the destination's local time
Recover from jet lag over the next day or two

questions.memo: First you board, then fly across zones, then reset your watch on arrival, and finally recover from jet lag.

questions.question: Lines that run from the North to the South Pole and measure position east or west are lines of _________.
questions.memo: Lines of longitude run north-south between the poles and measure how far east or west a place is.

questions.question: Why do countries far apart often experience different seasons at the same time of year?
options: Places in opposite hemispheres have opposite seasons
The international date line causes seasons
questions.expected: Places in opposite hemispheres have opposite seasons
questions.memo: The northern and southern hemispheres have opposite seasons, so it can be summer in one and winter in the other.

questions.question: True or false: A time zone map helps a traveller work out the local time at their destination.
questions.memo: A time zone map shows each region's offset from UTC, which the traveller uses to find local times.

questions.question: A flight leaves Johannesburg at 08:00 and the journey takes 11 hours. Ignoring any time-zone change, what is the flying (elapsed) time on arrival?
questions.memo: Flying time is simply how long the flight lasts — 11 hours — separate from any change in local clock time.

questions.question: Which symptom is typical of jet lag?
options: Tiredness and difficulty sleeping at the right local time
questions.expected: Tiredness and difficulty sleeping at the right local time
questions.memo: Jet lag commonly causes tiredness and trouble sleeping because the body clock is out of step with local time.

TOUR.G12.T2.ICONS.A1.title: World-famous icons & attractions
TOUR.G12.T2.ICONS.A1.description: The difference between an attraction and an icon; why certain attractions or physical features are regarded as icons; the location (country and city/area) of world-famous icons such as the Eiffel Tower, Taj Mahal, Great Wall of China, Statue of Liberty, Sydney Opera House, Christ the Redeemer, Colosseum, Big Ben, the Pyramids of Giza and Machu Picchu; and the economic significance of icons for a country.
TOUR.G12.T2.ICONS.A1.recovery_strategy: Learn each icon as a pair: icon → country (and city). An icon is more than an attraction — it is instantly recognised and stands as a symbol of its country, e.g. Eiffel Tower → Paris, France.

questions.question: What is the difference between a tourist attraction and an icon?
options: An icon is a famous, instantly recognised attraction that symbolises its country or city
An icon is always smaller than an attraction
An icon is a type of foreign currency
There is no difference at all
questions.expected: An icon is a famous, instantly recognised attraction that symbolises its country or city
questions.memo: All icons are attractions, but an icon is so famous and recognisable that it stands as a symbol of its country or city.

questions.question: In which country is the Eiffel Tower found?
questions.memo: The Eiffel Tower is in Paris, France, and is one of the world's most recognised icons.

questions.question: The Taj Mahal is a world-famous icon located in:
questions.memo: The Taj Mahal is in Agra, India — a cultural icon and World Heritage Site.

questions.question: The Great Wall is a famous icon found in _________.
questions.memo: The Great Wall of China stretches across northern China and is a world icon.

questions.question: The Statue of Liberty stands in which city?
questions.memo: The Statue of Liberty is in New York, in the United States of America.

questions.question: True or false: The Sydney Opera House is an icon located in Australia.
questions.memo: The Sydney Opera House is in Sydney, Australia, and is a world-famous icon.

questions.question: The Statue of Christ the Redeemer overlooks which city?
questions.memo: Christ the Redeemer (Corcovado) stands above Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.

questions.question: Sort each icon under the country where it is found.
questions.memo: The Colosseum and Leaning Tower are in Italy; the Pyramids and Sphinx in Egypt; Big Ben and Buckingham Palace in the United Kingdom.

questions.question: Why are icons economically significant for a country?
options: They attract many tourists, who spend money and create jobs
They make the local currency stronger overnight
They remove the need for any other attractions
They lower the country's electricity bill
questions.expected: They attract many tourists, who spend money and create jobs
questions.memo: Famous icons draw large numbers of visitors whose spending supports income and jobs in the local economy.

questions.question: Machu Picchu, a famous icon high in the Andes mountains, is in which country?
questions.memo: Machu Picchu is an ancient Inca site near Cuzco in Peru.

questions.question: The ancient amphitheatre known as the _________ is a famous icon in Rome, Italy.
questions.memo: The Colosseum is the great Roman amphitheatre in Rome and a major Italian icon.

questions.question: The Great Pyramids and the Sphinx are icons found near which city?
questions.memo: The Pyramids of Giza and the Sphinx are located near Cairo, Egypt.

questions.question: True or false: The Parthenon is an ancient icon located in Athens, Greece.
questions.memo: The Parthenon is a temple on the Acropolis in Athens, Greece — a famous icon of the ancient world.

questions.question: Why is a famous icon often used in a country's tourism marketing?
options: It is instantly recognised and helps sell the destination
It increases the number of public holidays
It replaces the need for an airport
It changes the country's time zone
questions.expected: It is instantly recognised and helps sell the destination
questions.memo: Because icons are instantly recognised, they are powerful symbols used to market a destination.

questions.question: The clock tower commonly called _________ stands beside the Houses of Parliament in London.
questions.memo: Big Ben (the Palace of Westminster's clock tower) is a famous London and UK icon.

questions.question: The Christ the Redeemer statue and the Eiffel Tower share which feature that makes them icons?
options: They are world-famous symbols closely linked to their cities
They are both located in Africa
They are both natural rock formations
They are both less than ten years old
questions.expected: They are world-famous symbols closely linked to their cities
questions.memo: Both are instantly recognised symbols strongly associated with their cities (Rio and Paris), which is what makes them icons.

questions.question: The ancient rock-carved city of Petra is a famous icon in:
questions.memo: Petra is the ancient stone-carved city in Jordan, a well-known world icon.

questions.question: Sort each icon under whether it is a HUMAN-MADE structure or a NATURAL feature.
questions.memo: The Eiffel Tower, Great Wall and Taj Mahal are built by people; Everest, Niagara Falls and Uluru are natural features.

questions.question: True or false: An icon helps build a country's image and draws international visitors.
questions.memo: Icons strengthen a country's image abroad and attract international tourists, supporting the tourism economy.

questions.question: Niagara Falls, a famous natural icon, lies on the border between the United States and:
questions.memo: Niagara Falls is on the border of the United States and Canada and is a well-known natural icon.

TOUR.G12.T2.ATTRSUCCESS.A1.title: Factors contributing to the success of a tourist attraction
TOUR.G12.T2.ATTRSUCCESS.A1.description: Factors behind a successful attraction (excellent marketing, sustainable and responsible management, efficient and ethical staff, positive visitor experience, safety and crime prevention, good appearance and upkeep, universal access for people with disabilities) and the characteristics of success (visitor numbers exceed targets, repeat visits, income exceeds target, positive impact on the local community and environment).
TOUR.G12.T2.ATTRSUCCESS.A1.recovery_strategy: Separate cause from result: FACTORS are things management does (market well, keep it safe and clean, train staff); CHARACTERISTICS are measurable results (visitor numbers and income beat targets, visitors return).

questions.question: Which of these is a FACTOR that helps make a tourist attraction successful?
options: Letting the attraction become dirty and unsafe
Refusing entry to people with disabilities
questions.memo: Strong marketing draws visitors and is one of the factors that contributes to an attraction's success.

questions.question: Which of these is a CHARACTERISTIC showing that an attraction IS successful?
options: There is no safety or crime prevention
questions.memo: Beating the target number of visitors is a measurable sign (characteristic) that an attraction is successful.

questions.question: True or false: Good safety and crime prevention is a factor that contributes to a successful attraction.
questions.memo: Visitors return to and recommend places where they feel safe, so safety and crime prevention support success.

questions.question: Designing an attraction so that wheelchair users and others can move around easily provides _________ access.
questions.memo: Universal access means everyone, including people with disabilities, can use the attraction — a factor in its success.

questions.question: When visitors return to an attraction again and again, these are called:
questions.memo: Repeat visits — visitors coming back — are a characteristic of a successful attraction.

questions.question: Why does the general appearance and upkeep of an attraction matter for its success?
options: A clean, well-kept attraction gives a positive experience and draws repeat visits
Appearance has no effect on visitor numbers
Upkeep only matters for the staff car park
questions.expected: A clean, well-kept attraction gives a positive experience and draws repeat visits
questions.memo: A well-maintained, attractive site improves the visitor experience, encouraging people to return and recommend it.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis by choosing the strong supporting points.
questions.thesis: Good management is key to the success of a tourist attraction.

pool.text: It keeps the attraction clean, safe and well maintained
It markets the attraction well so more visitors come
It trains staff to be efficient and ethical, improving the visitor experience
It changes the country's time zone
It decides the colour of foreign bank notes

questions.memo: The strong points all describe what good management does — upkeep, marketing, staff training. The red herrings have nothing to do with managing an attraction.

questions.question: Sort each item under whether it is a FACTOR that creates success or a CHARACTERISTIC of a successful attraction.
questions.memo: Factors are things management does (marketing, staff, safety, upkeep). Characteristics are measurable results (visitors and income beating targets, repeat visits).

questions.question: True or false: When the income an attraction generates exceeds its target figures, this is a sign of success.
questions.memo: Income exceeding the target is a measurable characteristic of a successful attraction.

questions.question: How does ethical behaviour by staff and management help an attraction succeed?
options: It builds trust and a good reputation, encouraging visitors to return
It puts visitors off coming back
It has no effect on the attraction
It increases the price of fuel
questions.expected: It builds trust and a good reputation, encouraging visitors to return
questions.memo: Ethical, honest behaviour builds trust and reputation, which supports repeat visits and long-term success.

questions.question: A management plan that protects the environment and the local community is described as a _________ management plan.
questions.memo: Sustainable and responsible management protects the environment and community, helping the attraction succeed long-term.

questions.question: Which of these BEST shows a positive visitor experience?
options: Visitors enjoy their time and recommend the attraction to others
Visitors feel unsafe the whole time
questions.expected: Visitors enjoy their time and recommend the attraction to others
questions.memo: A positive experience means visitors enjoy themselves and recommend the attraction, supporting its success.

questions.question: True or false: Considering the needs of people with disabilities is a factor that helps an attraction succeed.
questions.memo: Providing universal access widens the market and improves the experience, contributing to success.

questions.question: An attraction has a positive impact on its local community when:
options: It creates jobs and supports local businesses
It forces local people to move away
It pollutes the area and creates no jobs
It keeps all its income overseas
questions.expected: It creates jobs and supports local businesses
questions.memo: A positive community impact — jobs and support for local business — is a characteristic of a successful, responsible attraction.

questions.question: Efficient and friendly _________ improve the visitor's experience and help an attraction succeed.
questions.memo: Efficient, friendly staff are a key factor in giving visitors a positive experience.

questions.question: Why might an attraction set a 'target number of visitors'?
options: To measure whether it is meeting its goals and succeeding
To decide the country's exchange rate
questions.expected: To measure whether it is meeting its goals and succeeding
questions.memo: A target lets management measure success — exceeding the target shows the attraction is doing well.

questions.question: Which combination would most likely make an attraction UNsuccessful?
options: Poor marketing, unsafe surroundings and unfriendly staff
Strong marketing, safety and friendly staff
questions.expected: Poor marketing, unsafe surroundings and unfriendly staff
questions.memo: Weak marketing, poor safety and unfriendly staff drive visitors away, leading to failure.

questions.question: True or false: A successful attraction usually has a positive impact on the local environment as well as the economy.
questions.memo: A successful, responsibly run attraction benefits both the local economy and environment.

questions.question: Marketing an attraction both locally AND internationally helps because:
options: It reaches a wider audience of possible visitors
It hides the attraction from tourists
It removes the need for upkeep
It lowers the quality of service
questions.expected: It reaches a wider audience of possible visitors
questions.memo: Marketing both at home and abroad reaches more potential visitors, supporting the attraction's success.

questions.question: Which statement correctly links a FACTOR to its RESULT?
options: Good upkeep and marketing (factors) lead to more repeat visits (result)
Repeat visits (factor) cause the attraction to be built (result)
Exceeding income targets (factor) creates the marketing plan (result)
Visitor numbers (factor) decide the country's time zone (result)
questions.expected: Good upkeep and marketing (factors) lead to more repeat visits (result)
questions.memo: Factors such as upkeep and marketing are causes; results such as repeat visits and higher income are the measurable outcomes.

TOUR.G12.T2.TOURPLAN.A1.title: Tour plans & route planning
TOUR.G12.T2.TOURPLAN.A1.description: Developing a tour plan to suit a tourist's profile, budget and available time; route planning; and choosing transport, accommodation, attractions and activities that match the customers' needs and preferences.
TOUR.G12.T2.TOURPLAN.A1.recovery_strategy: Start from the tourist PROFILE (who they are, how much money and time they have, what they like), then choose transport, accommodation and activities to fit it. The plan must suit the tourist, not the other way round.

questions.question: What should a tour plan be based on first?
options: The tourist's profile, budget and available time
The cheapest option regardless of the tourist
questions.expected: The tourist's profile, budget and available time
questions.memo: A good tour plan starts from who the tourist is, how much money they have and how much time, then fits choices to that.

questions.question: A backpacker on a tight budget wants a two-week trip. Which plan suits them BEST?
options: Hostels, public transport and free or low-cost attractions
questions.expected: Hostels, public transport and free or low-cost attractions
questions.memo: The plan must match the tourist's profile and budget — affordable options suit a budget backpacker.

questions.question: What does 'route planning' involve?
options: Working out the best, most logical way to travel between stops
questions.expected: Working out the best, most logical way to travel between stops
questions.memo: Route planning is mapping the most sensible, efficient path between the places on the tour.

questions.question: A plan must suit the tourist's needs and _________ — what they like and want.
questions.memo: Tour choices should match the tourist's needs and preferences (what they like and want from the trip).

questions.question: True or false: A good route plan avoids unnecessary backtracking between stops.
questions.memo: Avoiding backtracking saves time and money, so a good route plan keeps travel logical and efficient.

questions.question: A family with young children is planning a tour. Which choice best suits their profile?
options: Family-friendly accommodation and activities with shorter travel times
Late-night clubs and long all-day drives
A schedule with no rest stops
questions.expected: Family-friendly accommodation and activities with shorter travel times
questions.memo: A plan for a family with children should suit their profile: child-friendly options and manageable travel times.

questions.question: Sort each choice under whether it suits a LUXURY traveller or a BUDGET traveller.
questions.memo: Match each choice to the traveller's budget: high-cost options suit luxury travellers; low-cost options suit budget travellers.

questions.question: Why must available TIME be considered when planning a tour?
options: So the plan fits sensibly into the days available without rushing
Because time decides the exchange rate
Because it sets the company logo
It does not need to be considered
questions.expected: So the plan fits sensibly into the days available without rushing
questions.memo: The number of days available limits how much can be included, so the plan must fit the time without rushing.

questions.question: A tourist profile interested in history and culture should be offered:
options: Museums, heritage sites and cultural tours
questions.expected: Museums, heritage sites and cultural tours
questions.memo: Choices of attractions and activities should match the tourist's interests — history and culture here.

questions.question: Transport, accommodation and activities chosen in a tour plan should all match the tourist's _________.
questions.memo: Every choice in a tour plan should suit the tourist's profile — who they are and what they want.

questions.question: True or false: When planning a tour, the choice of transport should suit both the budget and the tourist's comfort needs.
questions.memo: Transport choices balance cost (budget) and the tourist's comfort and preferences.

questions.question: A tour route runs Cape Town → George → Knysna → Port Elizabeth along the coast. Why is this a logical route?
options: The stops follow one direction along the coast without doubling back
It crosses the same town three times
It flies the group overseas in between
It ignores where the stops actually are
questions.expected: The stops follow one direction along the coast without doubling back
questions.memo: A logical route moves steadily in one direction, linking nearby stops without backtracking.

questions.question: Which resource is MOST useful for route planning a road tour of South Africa?
options: A colour road map of South Africa
questions.expected: A colour road map of South Africa
questions.memo: A road map shows roads and distances between towns, which is essential for planning a sensible route.

questions.question: An adventure-loving tourist with a generous budget would best suit a plan with:
options: Activities such as bungee jumping, hiking and white-water rafting
questions.expected: Activities such as bungee jumping, hiking and white-water rafting
questions.memo: Activities should match the tourist's interests; an adventure lover suits active, outdoor experiences.

questions.question: Choosing accommodation that fits the tourist's budget and _________ is part of good tour planning.
questions.memo: Accommodation should match the tourist's budget and needs (such as family rooms or accessibility).

questions.question: Why should a tour planner use brochures of accommodation and attractions?
options: To compare options and choose those that suit the tourist
To replace the road map entirely
questions.expected: To compare options and choose those that suit the tourist
questions.memo: Brochures help the planner compare accommodation and attractions and pick the ones that fit the tourist's profile and budget.

questions.question: True or false: A tour plan that ignores the budget but matches everything else is still a good plan.
questions.memo: A plan that exceeds the budget is not workable. The plan must suit the tourist's profile, budget AND time.

questions.question: A group has only three days but wants to see attractions spread far apart. The planner should:
options: Choose attractions close together so they fit the available time
Promise everything and run hopelessly behind schedule
Cancel the tour with no explanation
questions.expected: Choose attractions close together so they fit the available time
questions.memo: Limited time means choosing attractions that fit realistically, often those nearer one another.

questions.question: Which question best helps build a tourist's profile before planning?
options: What are your interests, budget and how long can you travel?
Which World Heritage Sites are natural?
What is the capital of France?
questions.expected: What are your interests, budget and how long can you travel?
questions.memo: Understanding interests, budget and time lets the planner build a profile and design a suitable tour.

questions.question: Sort each planning decision under the part of the tour plan it belongs to.

items.text: Hiring a coach for the group
Booking a guesthouse for the night

questions.memo: Coaches and flights are transport; guesthouses and lodges are accommodation; game reserves and museum tours are attractions and activities.

TOUR.G12.T2.ITINERARY.A1.title: Compiling a day-by-day itinerary
TOUR.G12.T2.ITINERARY.A1.description: The main aspects of an itinerary (transport, accommodation, attractions, activities and stops for meals); factors to consider when drawing one up (logical planning, sensible spread, variety and appropriateness); and arranging the days of a trip in a logical order.
TOUR.G12.T2.ITINERARY.A1.recovery_strategy: Plan in a logical line: group nearby places together, avoid backtracking, keep travel times sensible, and spread activities with variety and rest. An itinerary should flow smoothly day by day.

questions.question: What is a day-by-day itinerary?
options: A detailed plan showing what happens on each day of a trip
A list of foreign exchange rates
A map of world time zones
questions.expected: A detailed plan showing what happens on each day of a trip
questions.memo: An itinerary sets out, day by day, the transport, accommodation, attractions, activities and meals for a trip.

questions.question: Which of these is a main aspect that an itinerary should describe?
options: The exchange rate of the rand
questions.memo: The main aspects of an itinerary are transport, accommodation, attractions, activities and meal stops.

questions.question: True or false: A good itinerary includes stops for meals.
questions.memo: Meal stops are one of the main aspects of an itinerary, ensuring travellers are fed during the day.

questions.question: An itinerary should be arranged with _________ planning so the days flow sensibly.
questions.memo: Logical planning means the days are arranged in a sensible order that flows well and avoids backtracking.

questions.question: Why is variety important in a day-by-day itinerary?
options: It keeps the trip interesting and suits different tastes
It makes the trip more confusing on purpose
It removes the need for accommodation
It sets the country's time zone
questions.expected: It keeps the trip interesting and suits different tastes
questions.memo: A good spread and variety of activities keeps travellers engaged and caters to different interests.

questions.question: Put these activities for ONE day into a sensible time order from morning to night.
questions.memo: A logical day runs breakfast, morning activity, lunch, afternoon activity, then dinner and overnight stay.

questions.question: Which itinerary mistake shows poor logical planning?
options: Driving from Durban to Cape Town and back to Durban between two nearby stops
Grouping nearby attractions on the same day
Allowing time for meals and rest
Following the coast in one direction
questions.expected: Driving from Durban to Cape Town and back to Durban between two nearby stops
questions.memo: Backtracking across the country wastes time and money and shows poor logical planning.

questions.question: True or false: An itinerary should allow realistic travel times between stops.
questions.memo: Realistic travel times keep the schedule achievable and avoid an exhausting, rushed trip.

questions.question: A daily itinerary table usually has columns for the day, transport, accommodation, attractions, activities and:
questions.memo: An itinerary table commonly includes a budget column alongside transport, accommodation, attractions and activities.

questions.question: What does a good 'spread' of activities across the days mean?
options: Activities are balanced across the trip, not all crammed into one day
Every activity happens on the first day
There are no activities at all
The same activity repeats every day
questions.expected: Activities are balanced across the trip, not all crammed into one day
questions.memo: A good spread balances activities across the days so no single day is overloaded.

questions.question: Activities in an itinerary should be _________ for the tourists — suitable for their interests and abilities.
questions.memo: Appropriateness means choosing activities that suit the tourists' interests, ages and abilities.

questions.question: Why should an itinerary include where travellers will sleep each night?
options: So accommodation is booked and travellers know where they are staying
Because it sets the exchange rate
questions.expected: So accommodation is booked and travellers know where they are staying
questions.memo: Including accommodation each night ensures rooms are arranged and travellers know where they will stay.

questions.question: True or false: A logical itinerary groups attractions that are close together on the same day.
questions.memo: Grouping nearby attractions reduces travel and makes the day efficient — good logical planning.

questions.question: Put these days of a Garden Route tour in a sensible WEST-to-EAST order.
questions.memo: Travelling along the Garden Route from west to east, the order runs Cape Town, Mossel Bay, Knysna, then Port Elizabeth.

questions.question: Including rest time in an itinerary is important because:
options: Travellers can become exhausted if every day is too full
Rest time increases the exchange rate
It removes the need for meals
questions.expected: Travellers can become exhausted if every day is too full
questions.memo: Building in rest avoids exhaustion and keeps travellers enjoying the trip — part of sensible, logical planning.

questions.question: Which detail does NOT belong in a day-by-day travel itinerary?
options: The bank's profit forecast for next year
Where the group will have lunch
Which attraction the group will visit
questions.expected: The bank's profit forecast for next year
questions.memo: A travel itinerary covers transport, meals, attractions and accommodation — not a bank's profit forecast.

questions.question: An itinerary is drawn up 'according to a scenario'. What does this mean?
options: It is built to fit a specific situation, such as a particular group, budget and time
It is copied exactly from another country
questions.expected: It is built to fit a specific situation, such as a particular group, budget and time
questions.memo: Drawing up an itinerary for a scenario means tailoring it to a given group, budget, time and purpose.

questions.question: True or false: The 24-hour clock can be used in an itinerary to show times clearly, such as 14:30 for half past two in the afternoon.
questions.memo: The 24-hour clock removes confusion between morning and afternoon times in an itinerary.

questions.question: The main focus when drawing up an itinerary should be the logical _________, variety and appropriateness of activities.
questions.memo: The CAPS focus is the logical spread, variety and appropriateness of activities across the days.

questions.question: Which itinerary is better planned?
options: One that links nearby stops, balances activities and allows for meals and rest
One that zig-zags across the country each day
One that schedules ten attractions in a single morning
questions.expected: One that links nearby stops, balances activities and allows for meals and rest
questions.memo: A well-planned itinerary is logical and balanced, linking nearby stops and allowing time for meals and rest.

TOUR.G12.T2.BUDGET.A1.title: Compiling a tour budget
TOUR.G12.T2.BUDGET.A1.description: Factors influencing the development of a tour budget and drawing up a basic budget showing expenses for travel, accommodation, meals, entrance to attractions, shopping and tips; simple addition of costs and working out what fits within a given budget.
TOUR.G12.T2.BUDGET.A1.recovery_strategy: List every cost type (travel, accommodation, meals, attractions, shopping, tips), add them up carefully, then compare the total with the money available. If it is over budget, cut or downgrade an item.

questions.question: What is a tour budget?
options: A plan of the expected costs of a tour
A map showing the tour route
A list of the world's time zones
A passport for the tour group
questions.expected: A plan of the expected costs of a tour
questions.memo: A tour budget lists and totals the expected costs so the tour can be planned within the money available.

questions.question: Which of these is a cost that should appear in a tour budget?
questions.memo: Accommodation is one of the main tour costs, along with travel, meals, attractions, shopping and tips.

questions.question: A budget lists travel R500, accommodation R800 and meals R300. What is the total?
questions.memo: Add the costs: R500 + R800 + R300 = R1 600.

questions.question: Small amounts given to thank service staff, included in a tour budget, are called _________.
questions.memo: Tips (gratuities) for service staff are one of the items included in a tour budget.

questions.question: True or false: A tour budget should include entrance fees to the attractions visited.
questions.memo: Entrance fees to attractions are a standard cost item in a tour budget.

questions.question: A tourist has R2 000. Travel costs R700, accommodation R900 and meals R250. How much is left for shopping and tips?
questions.memo: Total spent so far: R700 + R900 + R250 = R1 850. R2 000 − R1 850 = R150 left.

questions.question: Sort each item under whether it is a TOUR COST or NOT a tour cost.
questions.memo: Accommodation, travel, meals and entrance fees are real tour costs; a colour preference or the weather are not costs.

questions.question: Which factor would INCREASE the cost of a tour budget?
questions.memo: Luxury accommodation costs more, raising the total budget. Budget options lower it.

questions.question: A budget comes to R1 200 over the money available. What is the BEST first step?
options: Cut or downgrade some costs to fit the budget
Ignore the shortfall and hope it works out
questions.expected: Cut or downgrade some costs to fit the budget
questions.memo: When over budget, reduce or downgrade costs (cheaper accommodation, fewer paid activities) until the total fits.

questions.question: Money spent on souvenirs and gifts during a tour falls under the budget item:
questions.memo: Souvenirs and gifts are part of the shopping item in a tour budget.

questions.question: A tour budget lists costs so the planner can compare the total with the money _________.
questions.memo: The total is compared with the money available to check the tour is affordable.

questions.question: Travel R400, accommodation R600, meals R200, attractions R150, tips R50. What is the total budget?
questions.memo: Add all items: R400 + R600 + R200 + R150 + R50 = R1 400.

questions.question: True or false: Leaving out an expected cost makes a budget less accurate and risks running short of money.
questions.memo: Missing out a real cost understates the total, so the traveller may run short. Include every cost.

questions.question: Which factor influences the development of a tour budget?
options: The length of the tour and number of travellers
The colour of the tour bus
questions.expected: The length of the tour and number of travellers
questions.memo: Longer tours and more travellers raise total costs, so they strongly influence the budget.

questions.question: If a group of 4 each pays R250 for an activity, the total cost for the group is _________.
questions.memo: 4 travellers × R250 = R1 000 for the group.

questions.question: Why is a realistic tour budget important for a tourist?
options: So they do not run out of money during the trip
So they can ignore the exchange rate
So they can avoid carrying a passport
questions.expected: So they do not run out of money during the trip
questions.memo: A realistic budget helps the tourist plan their spending and avoid running out of money.

questions.question: A tourist wants to cut their budget. Which change saves the MOST without cancelling the trip?
options: Choosing cheaper accommodation for several nights
questions.expected: Choosing cheaper accommodation for several nights
questions.memo: Accommodation over several nights is a large cost, so downgrading it saves the most.

questions.question: True or false: A tour budget can include a small amount set aside for unexpected costs.
questions.memo: Allowing for unexpected costs makes a budget safer and more realistic.

questions.question: Sort each budget item under whether it is usually a LARGE cost or a SMALL cost on a tour.

items.text: Daily meals for the whole trip

questions.memo: Accommodation, transport and meals across a trip are large costs; a single tip, postcard or bottle of water are small costs.

questions.question: A budget of R3 000 has R2 700 of costs listed. How much is still unspent?
questions.memo: R3 000 − R2 700 = R300 still available.

TOUR.G12.T2.HEALTHSAFE.A1.title: Health & safety for travellers
TOUR.G12.T2.HEALTHSAFE.A1.description: Health concepts (World Health Organisation, health certificates, travel clinics, compulsory and recommended vaccinations such as yellow fever); precautions for high-risk areas (malaria, bilharzia, cholera; bottled water, sun block, preventative medicine); and general safety precautions for tourists in a car, in public, in a hotel room, at the airport and after dark.
TOUR.G12.T2.HEALTHSAFE.A1.recovery_strategy: HEALTH precautions protect against illness (vaccinations, tablets, bottled water); SAFETY precautions protect against crime and accidents (lock doors, don't flash valuables, be careful after dark). Ask: illness or harm?

questions.question: What does the World Health Organisation (WHO) do?
options: It guides international public health and advises on disease and vaccinations
It sets the exchange rate of currencies
It awards star gradings to hotels
questions.expected: It guides international public health and advises on disease and vaccinations
questions.memo: The WHO is the international body that guides public health and advises travellers on health risks and vaccinations.

questions.question: Where can a traveller get vaccinations and health advice before an overseas trip?
questions.memo: Travel clinics provide vaccinations, health certificates and advice for travellers.

questions.question: A vaccination that a country REQUIRES before you may enter is described as:
questions.memo: A compulsory vaccination is one you must have to enter a country, such as yellow fever for some destinations.

questions.question: In a malaria-risk area, travellers are advised to take preventative _________ as a health precaution.
questions.memo: Preventative medicine (such as anti-malaria tablets) is a key health precaution in malaria areas.

questions.question: True or false: Drinking bottled water is a sensible health precaution in some high-risk destinations.
questions.memo: Bottled water helps avoid illness from unsafe tap water — a recommended health precaution.

questions.question: Sort each precaution under whether it protects HEALTH (illness) or SAFETY (crime/accidents).

items.text: Do not display valuables in public
Keep car doors locked while driving

questions.memo: Health precautions guard against illness (tablets, water, vaccines); safety precautions guard against crime and accidents (locking doors, hiding valuables).

questions.question: Which vaccination is commonly required before entering certain high-risk tropical areas?
questions.memo: A yellow fever vaccination and certificate are required for entry to or from some high-risk areas.

questions.question: Why is the safety of tourists in South Africa important?
options: Tourists who feel safe return and recommend the country, supporting tourism
It increases the number of public holidays
It changes the country's time zone
questions.expected: Tourists who feel safe return and recommend the country, supporting tourism
questions.memo: Tourist safety protects the country's reputation; safe tourists return and recommend it, helping the tourism industry.

questions.question: Which is a sensible SAFETY precaution for a tourist after dark?
options: Avoid walking alone in unfamiliar, poorly lit areas
Carry all your cash openly in your hand
Leave the hotel room door wide open
questions.expected: Avoid walking alone in unfamiliar, poorly lit areas
questions.memo: Staying out of unfamiliar, dark areas alone reduces the risk of crime — a basic safety precaution.

questions.question: A document proving a traveller has had a required vaccination is a health _________.
questions.memo: A health certificate proves a traveller has received a required vaccination, such as for yellow fever.

questions.question: True or false: Using sun block is a health precaution for tourists visiting hot, sunny destinations.
questions.memo: Sun block protects against sunburn and skin damage — a sensible health precaution in sunny areas.

questions.question: Which water-borne illness is a risk in some areas, making clean water important?
questions.memo: Cholera is a water-borne disease, so clean, bottled water is an important precaution in risk areas.

questions.question: A safety precaution for a tourist in a car is to:
options: Keep doors locked and valuables out of sight
Leave the windows fully open with bags on the seat
Display expensive items on the dashboard
questions.expected: Keep doors locked and valuables out of sight
questions.memo: Locked doors and hidden valuables reduce the risk of theft, especially at traffic stops.

questions.question: True or false: A vaccination that is advised but not required is called a recommended vaccination.
questions.memo: A recommended vaccination is advised for protection but is not compulsory for entry.

questions.question: A bite from a mosquito in certain areas can spread which disease, calling for precautions?
questions.memo: Malaria is spread by mosquito bites in certain areas, so travellers take tablets and avoid bites.

questions.question: A safety precaution for a tourist in a hotel room is to:
options: Use the safe for valuables and keep the door locked
Leave the door open while out
Leave cash and a passport on the bed
questions.expected: Use the safe for valuables and keep the door locked
questions.memo: Locking the door and using the room safe protects a tourist's belongings.

questions.question: Tourists should take precautions at the _________ too, watching their luggage and documents in busy areas.
questions.memo: Busy airports are places where bags and documents can be lost or stolen, so vigilance is a safety precaution.

questions.question: True or false: Inbound tourists may be advised about health risks such as TB and HIV/Aids when visiting.
questions.memo: TB and HIV/Aids are health risks travellers may be informed about; awareness and precautions matter.

questions.question: Which combination correctly pairs a precaution with its TYPE?
options: Anti-malaria tablets — health; locking the car — safety
Anti-malaria tablets — safety; locking the car — health
questions.expected: Anti-malaria tablets — health; locking the car — safety
questions.memo: Tablets protect against illness (health); locking the car protects against crime (safety).

questions.question: Why should a traveller check health requirements well BEFORE departure?
options: Some vaccinations must be given days or weeks in advance to work
Because the exchange rate changes daily
Because time zones change health rules
questions.expected: Some vaccinations must be given days or weeks in advance to work
questions.memo: Certain vaccinations need time to take effect, so travellers must arrange them well before departure.

TOUR.G12.T2.TRAVELDOC.A1.title: Travel documentation
TOUR.G12.T2.TRAVELDOC.A1.description: Travel documents needed to visit a country (valid passport, visa, health certificate); obtaining a passport, visa and international driver's licence; and customs concepts — duty-free goods, prohibited goods, the green and red channels, to declare and travel allowances.
TOUR.G12.T2.TRAVELDOC.A1.recovery_strategy: GREEN channel = nothing to declare; RED channel = goods to declare or over the allowance. A passport identifies you; a visa is permission to enter a specific country. Match each document and channel to its job.

questions.question: Which document identifies a traveller and is needed to cross international borders?
questions.memo: A valid passport identifies the traveller and is required to travel between countries.

questions.question: What is a visa?
options: Official permission to enter a particular country
A type of credit card only
A road map of the country
questions.expected: Official permission to enter a particular country
questions.memo: A visa is permission, usually stamped or stuck in the passport, allowing entry to a specific country.

questions.question: At customs, which channel should a traveller with NOTHING to declare use?
questions.memo: The green channel is for travellers with nothing to declare; the red channel is for those with goods to declare.

questions.question: A traveller carrying goods above the allowance, or goods to declare, must use the _________ channel.
questions.memo: The red channel is for travellers who have goods to declare or who exceed their duty-free allowance.

questions.question: True or false: A South African may need a visa to visit some countries but not others.
questions.memo: Visa requirements vary by country; some require a visa, others allow visa-free entry for South Africans.

questions.question: Goods on which no import duty (tax) is charged, up to a limit, are called _________ goods.
questions.memo: Duty-free goods can be brought in without paying import duty, up to a set allowance.

questions.question: Items that may NOT be brought into a country at all are called:
questions.memo: Prohibited goods are banned items that may not be brought into the country under any circumstances.

questions.question: Sort each customs term under its correct meaning.

items.text: A bottle of perfume within the limit
A few souvenirs within the allowance

questions.memo: Goods within the duty-free allowance are allowed; prohibited goods and anything over the allowance must be declared or are banned.

questions.question: To drive legally in many foreign countries, a tourist should obtain an:
questions.memo: An international driver's licence allows a tourist to drive legally in many other countries.

questions.question: True or false: A passport should be valid for the whole period of travel and often some months beyond.
questions.memo: Many countries require a passport to remain valid for several months beyond the trip, so travellers must check the expiry date.

questions.question: To 'declare' goods at customs means to:
options: Tell the customs officials what dutiable or restricted goods you are carrying
Sell your goods at the airport
questions.expected: Tell the customs officials what dutiable or restricted goods you are carrying
questions.memo: To declare means to openly tell customs about goods that may be taxed or restricted.

questions.question: Which document might a traveller need in addition to a passport for some destinations?
options: A health certificate (e.g. for yellow fever)
A copy of their school report
questions.expected: A health certificate (e.g. for yellow fever)
questions.memo: Some countries require a health certificate (such as yellow fever) along with the passport and visa.

questions.question: The limit on the value or quantity of goods a traveller may bring in duty-free is called the travel _________.
questions.memo: A travel allowance is the limit of goods a traveller may bring in without paying duty.
