questions.question: Where would a South African apply for a passport?
questions.memo: Passports in South Africa are issued by the Department of Home Affairs.

questions.question: True or false: Choosing the wrong customs channel, such as the green channel when you have goods to declare, can lead to penalties.
questions.memo: Using the green channel with goods to declare breaks customs rules and can result in fines or penalties.

questions.question: Which set of documents would a tourist typically need to visit a foreign country that requires a visa?
options: A valid passport and a visa (and any required health certificate)
questions.expected: A valid passport and a visa (and any required health certificate)
questions.memo: For a visa-required country, the traveller needs a valid passport, a visa, and any health certificate required.

questions.question: When completing a visa application form, a traveller should:
options: Fill in all sections truthfully and accurately
Give false information to speed it up
questions.expected: Fill in all sections truthfully and accurately
questions.memo: Visa forms must be completed fully and honestly; false information can lead to refusal or penalties.

questions.question: Sort each item under whether it is a TRAVEL DOCUMENT or NOT a travel document.
questions.memo: Passports, visas, health certificates and international driver's licences are travel documents; a menu or shopping receipt is not.

questions.question: Why do customs regulations exist when arriving in or leaving South Africa?
options: To control which goods may be brought in or taken out and to collect any duty owed
questions.expected: To control which goods may be brought in or taken out and to collect any duty owed
questions.memo: Customs regulations control the movement of goods across the border and ensure any duty is paid.

questions.question: A traveller buys perfume and a camera abroad worth far more than the duty-free allowance. On return they should:
options: Use the red channel and declare the goods
Use the green channel and say nothing
Hide the goods in their luggage
Throw the goods away before landing
questions.expected: Use the red channel and declare the goods
questions.memo: Goods above the duty-free allowance must be declared in the red channel, where any duty is paid.

TOUR.G12.T3.WHSUNESCO.A1.title: World Heritage Sites & the role of UNESCO
TOUR.G12.T3.WHSUNESCO.A1.description: The concept of a World Heritage Site; the role of UNESCO (its logo and main function of identifying and protecting sites of outstanding universal value); the difference between natural and cultural World Heritage Sites; and the value of World Heritage status to a country's tourism industry.
TOUR.G12.T3.WHSUNESCO.A1.strand: Term 3 — World Heritage Sites, foreign exchange & international travel
TOUR.G12.T3.WHSUNESCO.A1.recovery_strategy: UNESCO (a United Nations body) declares and protects World Heritage Sites — not the site owner. NATURAL = made by nature (landscapes, fossils, wetlands); CULTURAL = made by people (buildings, rock art, settlements).

questions.question: What is a World Heritage Site?
options: A place of outstanding universal value protected for future generations
Any hotel with a five-star grading
questions.expected: A place of outstanding universal value protected for future generations
questions.memo: A World Heritage Site is a place of outstanding universal value, recognised and protected so it survives for future generations.

questions.question: Which organisation identifies and protects World Heritage Sites?
questions.memo: UNESCO, a United Nations body, identifies, declares and helps protect World Heritage Sites.

questions.question: True or false: A country can declare its own sites to be World Heritage Sites without UNESCO.
questions.memo: Only UNESCO can grant World Heritage status; a country may nominate a site, but UNESCO decides.

questions.question: A World Heritage Site created by nature, such as a wetland or mountain range, is a _________ site.
questions.memo: Natural World Heritage Sites are formed by nature — landscapes, ecosystems, fossils and similar.

questions.question: A World Heritage Site made by people, such as an old fort or rock art, is a _________ site.
questions.memo: Cultural World Heritage Sites are created by people — buildings, settlements, rock art and similar.

questions.question: What does UNESCO stand for in this context?
options: United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation
United National Economic and Social Council
Universal Nature and Eco Safety Council
United Nations Sport and Entertainment Committee
questions.expected: United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation
questions.memo: UNESCO is the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation, which protects World Heritage Sites.

questions.question: Sort each example under whether it is a NATURAL or a CULTURAL World Heritage Site.

items.text: An ancient prison island used in history
A mountain range and its ecosystems
Rock art painted by early people
A region of rare indigenous plants
The remains of an ancient kingdom's settlement

questions.memo: Natural sites are made by nature (wetlands, mountains, plant regions); cultural sites are made by people (prison island, rock art, settlements).

questions.question: What is the main function of UNESCO regarding heritage?
options: To identify, protect and preserve sites of outstanding universal value
To set the exchange rate of currencies
questions.expected: To identify, protect and preserve sites of outstanding universal value
questions.memo: UNESCO's main function is to identify, protect and preserve places of outstanding universal value as World Heritage Sites.

questions.question: True or false: World Heritage status can boost a site's tourism by raising its international profile.
questions.memo: World Heritage status raises a site's profile and prestige, attracting more international visitors and tourism income.

questions.question: Why is it valuable for a country's tourism to have World Heritage Sites?
options: They attract visitors, create jobs and bring in tourism income
They lower the price of fuel
They change the country's time zone
They remove the need for marketing
questions.expected: They attract visitors, create jobs and bring in tourism income
questions.memo: World Heritage Sites draw tourists, supporting jobs and income — a real value to the tourism industry.

questions.question: UNESCO is an agency of which larger international body?
questions.memo: UNESCO is a specialised agency of the United Nations.

questions.question: Sites are added to the World Heritage list only if they meet UNESCO's _________ of outstanding universal value.
questions.memo: A site must meet UNESCO's criteria for outstanding universal value to be listed.

questions.question: True or false: A site can be a 'mixed' World Heritage Site if it has both natural and cultural value.
questions.memo: Some sites are listed as mixed because they hold both natural and cultural value.

questions.question: Which best describes the difference between a natural and a cultural World Heritage Site?
options: Natural sites are formed by nature; cultural sites are created by people
Natural sites are always bigger than cultural sites
Cultural sites are always older than natural sites
questions.expected: Natural sites are formed by nature; cultural sites are created by people
questions.memo: Natural = made by nature; cultural = made by people. This is the key distinction.

questions.question: Why does UNESCO protect World Heritage Sites?
options: So they are preserved for future generations to enjoy and learn from
So they can be sold to the highest bidder
So they can be closed to all visitors forever
So they can be moved to another country
questions.expected: So they are preserved for future generations to enjoy and learn from
questions.memo: Protection ensures these special places survive and remain valuable for future generations.

questions.question: The UNESCO World Heritage emblem (logo) is meant to symbolise:
options: The link between cultural (human-made) and natural heritage
The exchange rate of the dollar
questions.expected: The link between cultural (human-made) and natural heritage
questions.memo: The emblem represents the connection between cultural and natural heritage that UNESCO protects.

questions.question: True or false: World Heritage Sites must be looked after responsibly so tourism does not damage them.
questions.memo: Responsible management is needed so visitor numbers and tourism do not harm these protected sites.

questions.question: Being listed as a World Heritage Site can help a place receive:
options: Greater recognition and sometimes funding to protect it
questions.expected: Greater recognition and sometimes funding to protect it
questions.memo: Listing brings recognition and can attract support and funding for the site's protection.

questions.question: A region famous for its rare and varied indigenous plant life would most likely be listed as a:
questions.memo: Rare plant life and ecosystems are natural features, so such a region would be a natural site.

questions.question: Which statement about UNESCO and World Heritage Sites is correct?
options: UNESCO lists sites of outstanding universal value to protect them for the world
UNESCO sells World Heritage Sites to tourists
UNESCO only protects sites in Europe
questions.expected: UNESCO lists sites of outstanding universal value to protect them for the world
questions.memo: UNESCO lists and protects sites of outstanding universal value across the whole world.

TOUR.G12.T3.WHSSA.A1.title: World Heritage Sites in South Africa
TOUR.G12.T3.WHSSA.A1.description: South Africa's World Heritage Sites and their type and location — the Cradle of Humankind, Robben Island, iSimangaliso (Greater St Lucia) Wetland Park, uKhahlamba-Drakensberg Park, Mapungubwe, the Cape Floral Region, the Vredefort Dome, the Richtersveld and the Barberton Makhonjwa Mountains — and how each meets UNESCO criteria.
TOUR.G12.T3.WHSSA.A1.strand: Term 3 — World Heritage Sites, foreign exchange & international travel
TOUR.G12.T3.WHSSA.A1.recovery_strategy: For each South African site, learn its type (natural or cultural) and province. Robben Island and Mapungubwe are cultural (human history); iSimangaliso and the Cape Floral Region are natural (ecosystems); the Cradle of Humankind (fossils) is in Gauteng.

questions.question: The Cradle of Humankind, famous for early human fossils, is found in which province?
questions.memo: The Cradle of Humankind, a cultural World Heritage Site rich in hominid fossils, is in Gauteng.

questions.question: Robben Island, where Nelson Mandela was imprisoned, is which TYPE of World Heritage Site?
questions.memo: Robben Island is a cultural site because of its human history, especially the imprisonment of political prisoners.

questions.question: The iSimangaliso (Greater St Lucia) Wetland Park is a _________ World Heritage Site.
questions.memo: iSimangaliso is a natural site, protected for its wetlands, estuaries and rich wildlife.

questions.question: In which province is Robben Island located?
questions.memo: Robben Island lies off the coast of Cape Town in the Western Cape.

questions.question: True or false: The Cape Floral Region is a natural World Heritage Site protected for its rich plant life (fynbos).
questions.memo: The Cape Floral Region is a natural site famous for its enormous variety of indigenous plants, including fynbos.

questions.question: Mapungubwe, the site of an ancient African kingdom, is which type of World Heritage Site?
questions.memo: Mapungubwe is a cultural site, the landscape of a powerful early African kingdom in Limpopo.

questions.question: Sort each South African World Heritage Site under whether it is NATURAL or CULTURAL.
questions.memo: Natural: iSimangaliso, Cape Floral Region, Vredefort Dome (made by nature). Cultural: Robben Island, Mapungubwe, Cradle of Humankind (human history).

questions.question: The Vredefort Dome, formed by a giant meteorite impact long ago, is a _________ site.
questions.memo: The Vredefort Dome is a natural site marking the world's largest known meteorite impact structure.

questions.question: The uKhahlamba-Drakensberg Park is recognised for BOTH its natural beauty and its:
questions.memo: The Drakensberg Park is a mixed site, valued for its mountain scenery and its ancient San rock art.

questions.question: True or false: South Africa has several World Heritage Sites, both natural and cultural.
questions.memo: South Africa has a number of World Heritage Sites, including both natural and cultural types.

questions.question: Which World Heritage Site is famous for fossils that show the origins of humankind?
questions.memo: The Cradle of Humankind is rich in early hominid fossils that reveal human origins.

questions.question: The iSimangaliso Wetland Park lies along the coast of which province?
questions.memo: iSimangaliso stretches along the KwaZulu-Natal coast.

questions.question: True or false: World Heritage status helps South Africa market these sites to international tourists.
questions.memo: World Heritage status raises the sites' profile, helping South Africa attract international visitors.

questions.question: The Richtersveld Cultural and Botanical Landscape protects the land and traditions of which people?
questions.memo: The Richtersveld is a cultural landscape protecting the land and traditional way of life of the Nama people.

questions.question: A site protected for its rich variety of indigenous plants is a _________ World Heritage Site.
questions.memo: Protecting plant life and ecosystems makes a site natural, like the Cape Floral Region.

questions.question: Why is it important that South Africa's World Heritage Sites are managed responsibly?
options: So tourism does not damage them and they last for future generations
So that fewer South Africans can visit them
So the exchange rate stays the same
So airports can be built on them
questions.expected: So tourism does not damage them and they last for future generations
questions.memo: Responsible management protects the sites from damage so they survive for future generations while still benefiting tourism.

questions.question: The Barberton Makhonjwa Mountains are valued as a World Heritage Site mainly for their:
options: Very ancient, well-preserved rocks and geology
questions.expected: Very ancient, well-preserved rocks and geology
questions.memo: The Barberton Makhonjwa Mountains are a natural site protecting some of the oldest, best-preserved geology on Earth.

questions.question: True or false: Robben Island and Mapungubwe are both cultural World Heritage Sites linked to human history.
questions.memo: Both are cultural sites: Robben Island for its prison history and Mapungubwe for its ancient kingdom.

questions.question: How do South Africa's World Heritage Sites benefit the tourism industry?
options: They draw visitors who spend money, creating jobs and income
They reduce the number of tourists each year
They replace the need for accommodation
They set the country's time zone
questions.expected: They draw visitors who spend money, creating jobs and income
questions.memo: The sites attract tourists whose spending supports jobs and income in the tourism industry.

questions.question: Which pairing of a South African site with its type is CORRECT?
options: Cape Floral Region — natural; Robben Island — cultural
Cape Floral Region — cultural; Robben Island — natural
questions.expected: Cape Floral Region — natural; Robben Island — cultural
questions.memo: The Cape Floral Region (plant life) is natural; Robben Island (human history) is cultural.

TOUR.G12.T3.RAND.A1.title: The strong & weak rand
TOUR.G12.T3.RAND.A1.description: The concepts of a strong and a weak rand; the relative strength or weakness of a currency at a given time; the link to gross domestic product (GDP) and the multiplier effect; and how a strong or weak rand affects the buying power of South Africans abroad and the cost of South Africa for inbound tourists.
TOUR.G12.T3.RAND.A1.strand: Term 3 — World Heritage Sites, foreign exchange & international travel
TOUR.G12.T3.RAND.A1.recovery_strategy: A STRONG rand buys more foreign currency — good for South Africans travelling out, but makes SA pricier for inbound tourists. A WEAK rand is the opposite: cheaper for inbound tourists, dearer for outbound South Africans. Ask who is travelling which way.

questions.question: What does it mean when we say the rand is 'strong'?
options: One rand buys more foreign currency than before
One rand buys less foreign currency than before
The rand has stopped working as money
The rand is heavier than other coins
questions.expected: One rand buys more foreign currency than before
questions.memo: A strong rand means each rand buys more foreign currency — its buying power abroad has risen.

questions.question: What does a 'weak' rand mean?
options: Each rand buys less foreign currency than before
Each rand buys more foreign currency than before
The rand can no longer be exchanged
The rand is only used for tips
questions.expected: Each rand buys less foreign currency than before
questions.memo: A weak rand means each rand buys less foreign currency — its buying power abroad has fallen.

questions.question: A strong rand is GOOD news for which tourists?
options: Foreign tourists coming to South Africa (inbound)
questions.memo: A strong rand buys more foreign currency, making overseas trips cheaper for outbound South Africans.

questions.question: A weak rand makes South Africa _________ for foreign (inbound) tourists.
questions.memo: A weak rand means foreigners get more rands for their money, so South Africa becomes cheaper to visit.

questions.question: True or false: A weak rand makes overseas holidays more expensive for South Africans.
questions.memo: A weak rand buys less foreign currency, so South Africans pay more for trips abroad.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis by choosing the strong supporting points.
questions.thesis: A weak rand can benefit South Africa's inbound tourism.

pool.text: Foreign tourists get more rands for their money, so South Africa is cheaper to visit
Cheaper prices attract more foreign arrivals, boosting tourism income
More inbound spending supports local jobs and businesses
The rand notes are printed in bright colours
Aeroplanes have many seats

questions.memo: The strong points trace a weak rand to cheaper prices, more arrivals and more local spending. The red herrings have nothing to do with the exchange rate.

questions.question: If R1 used to buy $0.07 and now buys $0.05, the rand has become:
questions.memo: Each rand now buys fewer dollars (0.05 instead of 0.07), so the rand has weakened.

questions.question: A strong rand tends to make South Africa _________ for inbound foreign tourists.
questions.memo: A strong rand means foreigners get fewer rands for their money, so South Africa becomes more expensive (dearer) to visit.

questions.question: True or false: A strong rand always benefits the South African tourism industry.
questions.memo: A strong rand makes South Africa pricier for inbound tourists, which can reduce foreign arrivals — not always good for tourism.

questions.question: What is gross domestic product (GDP)?
options: The total value of goods and services a country produces
The number of tourists who visit a single hotel
The strength of a single bank
The price of one airline ticket
questions.expected: The total value of goods and services a country produces
questions.memo: GDP measures the total value of goods and services produced in a country, to which tourism contributes.

questions.question: When tourism money is spent and re-spent through the economy, supporting more businesses, this is called the _________ effect.
questions.memo: The multiplier effect is the way tourist spending circulates and supports many businesses, adding to GDP.

questions.question: Why might a South African choose to travel locally rather than overseas when the rand is weak?
options: Overseas trips cost more, so local travel offers better value
Local travel needs no money at all
A weak rand bans overseas travel
Local travel changes the exchange rate
questions.expected: Overseas trips cost more, so local travel offers better value
questions.memo: A weak rand makes foreign trips dearer, so many South Africans choose better-value domestic travel.

questions.question: True or false: The strength of the rand can change from one day to the next.
questions.memo: Exchange rates change constantly, so the rand can be relatively stronger or weaker at different times.

questions.question: A foreign tourist finds their money buys far more in South Africa this year than last year. The rand has probably become:
questions.memo: If foreign money buys more rands and goods, the rand has weakened against that currency.

questions.question: How does a healthy tourism industry contribute to South Africa's GDP?
options: Tourist spending adds to the value of goods and services produced
Tourism removes money from the economy
Tourism has no link to GDP
questions.expected: Tourist spending adds to the value of goods and services produced
questions.memo: Tourist spending on transport, accommodation, food and activities adds to GDP and supports the economy.

questions.question: A strong rand affects an outbound South African tourist by:
options: Giving them more spending power abroad
questions.expected: Giving them more spending power abroad
questions.memo: A strong rand buys more foreign currency, so outbound South Africans have more to spend overseas.

questions.question: The terms 'strong' and 'weak' rand describe the rand's value compared with:
questions.memo: A strong or weak rand is always measured against other currencies, such as the dollar, pound or euro.

questions.question: True or false: A weak rand can encourage more foreign tourists to visit South Africa.
questions.memo: Because a weak rand makes South Africa cheaper for foreigners, it can attract more inbound tourists.

questions.question: Which statement correctly links rand strength to tourists?
options: Strong rand helps outbound South Africans; weak rand helps inbound foreigners
Strong rand helps inbound foreigners; weak rand helps outbound South Africans
Rand strength has no effect on any tourist
Both strong and weak rand harm all tourists equally
questions.expected: Strong rand helps outbound South Africans; weak rand helps inbound foreigners
questions.memo: A strong rand benefits South Africans going abroad; a weak rand benefits foreigners coming to South Africa.

questions.question: The 'buying power' of a currency means:
options: How much it can buy when exchanged for goods or other money
questions.expected: How much it can buy when exchanged for goods or other money
questions.memo: Buying power is how much a currency can purchase; a strong rand has greater buying power abroad.

TOUR.G12.T3.FOREX.A1.title: Currency conversions
TOUR.G12.T3.FOREX.A1.description: Reading a currency rate sheet and converting between South African rand and major currencies using rates given as 1 unit of foreign currency = a value in rand (e.g. 1 USD = R18). Working out how much foreign currency a rand amount buys, and how many rand a foreign amount costs, rounded to two decimals.
TOUR.G12.T3.FOREX.A1.strand: Term 3 — World Heritage Sites, foreign exchange & international travel
TOUR.G12.T3.FOREX.A1.recovery_strategy: Use the rate exactly as written in the question. If 1 USD = R18, then to find rand multiply dollars by 18; to find dollars divide rand by 18. Always check the answer makes sense in size.

questions.question: A currency rate sheet shows the rate as 1 USD = R18. What does this mean?
options: One US dollar can be exchanged for 18 rand
One rand can be exchanged for 18 dollars
The dollar and rand are equal in value
questions.expected: One US dollar can be exchanged for 18 rand
questions.memo: The rate 1 USD = R18 means each US dollar is worth 18 rand.

questions.question: If 1 USD = R20, how many rand do you need to buy 5 US dollars?
questions.memo: Multiply dollars by the rate: 5 × R20 = R100.

questions.question: If 1 USD = R10, how many dollars can you get for R100?
questions.memo: Divide rand by the rate: R100 ÷ R10 = $10.

questions.question: If R1 = $0.05, then R200 buys $_________.
questions.memo: Multiply rand by the rate per rand: 200 × 0.05 = $10.

questions.question: True or false: On a rate sheet, when 1 GBP = R23, one British pound is worth 23 rand.
questions.memo: The rate 1 GBP = R23 means each pound is worth 23 rand.

questions.question: If 1 EUR = R20, how many rand are needed for 10 euros?
questions.memo: Multiply euros by the rate: 10 × R20 = R200.

questions.question: If 1 USD = R25, how many dollars can a tourist get for R500?
questions.memo: Divide rand by the rate: R500 ÷ R25 = $20.

questions.question: Sort each currency amount under whether it is worth MORE or LESS than R100, given 1 USD = R20.
questions.memo: At R20 per dollar, R100 equals $5. Amounts above $5 are worth more than R100; amounts below $5 are worth less.

questions.question: If 1 AUD = R12, how many rand do you need for 3 Australian dollars?
questions.memo: Multiply: 3 × R12 = R36.

questions.question: To convert dollars INTO rand when 1 USD = R18, you should:
options: Multiply the number of dollars by 18
Divide the number of dollars by 18
Add 18 to the number of dollars
Subtract 18 from the number of dollars
questions.expected: Multiply the number of dollars by 18
questions.memo: Since each dollar is worth R18, multiply the dollar amount by 18 to get rand.

questions.question: To convert rand INTO dollars when 1 USD = R18, you should _________ the rand amount by 18.
questions.memo: Because each dollar costs R18, divide the rand amount by 18 to find how many dollars it buys.

questions.question: If 1 GBP = R20, how much in rand is 4 British pounds worth?
questions.memo: Multiply: 4 × R20 = R80.

questions.question: True or false: A currency rate sheet shows how much one unit of foreign currency is worth in rand.
questions.memo: A rate sheet lists the value of one unit of each foreign currency in rand, such as 1 USD = R18.

questions.question: If 1 USD = R20, a tourist with R1 000 can buy how many dollars?
If 1 EUR = R20, then R60 is equal to _________ euros.
questions.memo: Divide: R60 ÷ R20 = 3 euros.

questions.question: A tourist exchanges R400 at 1 USD = R10. How many dollars do they receive?
questions.memo: Divide: R400 ÷ R10 = $40.

questions.question: If 1 USD = R15, how much in rand will 2 dollars cost?
questions.memo: Multiply: 2 × R15 = R30.

questions.question: True or false: If the rate is 1 USD = R20, then R20 buys exactly one US dollar.
questions.memo: At 1 USD = R20, you pay R20 to buy one dollar, so R20 buys exactly $1.

questions.question: A souvenir costs $4. At 1 USD = R20, how much is that in rand?
questions.memo: Multiply: 4 × R20 = R80.

questions.question: Why is it important to round currency conversions to two decimals (e.g. R34.56)?
options: Money is counted in rands and cents, so two decimals give an exact amount
Because the time zone requires it
It is never important to round
questions.expected: Money is counted in rands and cents, so two decimals give an exact amount
questions.memo: Currency is measured in rands and cents (two decimals), so conversions are rounded to two decimals for accuracy.

TOUR.G12.T3.BSRBBR.A1.title: Bank selling rate vs bank buying rate
TOUR.G12.T3.BSRBBR.A1.description: The difference between the bank selling rate (BSR) and the bank buying rate (BBR); which rate applies when a traveller buys foreign currency before a trip and which applies when they sell unused foreign currency back; and why the two rates differ (the bank's margin).
TOUR.G12.T3.BSRBBR.A1.strand: Term 3 — World Heritage Sites, foreign exchange & international travel
TOUR.G12.T3.BSRBBR.A1.recovery_strategy: Read the rate from the BANK's point of view. BSR (bank SELLING) = the bank sells you foreign currency (you buy before the trip). BBR (bank BUYING) = the bank buys back your leftover foreign currency. The selling rate is less favourable to you.

questions.question: What does the bank selling rate (BSR) apply to?
options: When the bank SELLS foreign currency to a traveller
When the bank BUYS foreign currency from a traveller
When a traveller pays income tax
When a tourist books a hotel
questions.expected: When the bank SELLS foreign currency to a traveller
questions.memo: The bank selling rate applies when the bank sells you foreign currency — for example before you travel.

questions.question: What does the bank buying rate (BBR) apply to?
options: When the bank BUYS back foreign currency from a traveller
When the bank SELLS foreign currency to a traveller
When the bank lends money for a house
When a tourist pays for a tour
questions.expected: When the bank BUYS back foreign currency from a traveller
questions.memo: The bank buying rate applies when the bank buys your leftover foreign currency, for example after you return.

questions.question: Before a trip abroad, a traveller wants to buy US dollars. Which rate applies?
questions.memo: When the traveller buys foreign currency, the bank is selling it, so the bank selling rate (BSR) applies.

questions.question: After returning home with leftover dollars, a traveller sells them back to the bank. The bank uses its _________ rate.
questions.memo: When the bank buys the leftover currency from the traveller, the bank buying rate applies.

questions.question: True or false: The rates are named from the BANK'S point of view, not the customer's.
questions.memo: BSR and BBR describe what the BANK does — selling to or buying from the customer.

questions.question: Why do the bank's selling and buying rates differ?
options: The difference is the bank's margin (how it makes a profit on the exchange)
There is no reason; it is random
questions.expected: The difference is the bank's margin (how it makes a profit on the exchange)
questions.memo: Banks sell currency at a higher rate and buy it back at a lower rate; the gap is their profit margin.

questions.question: Sort each situation under whether the bank uses its SELLING rate or its BUYING rate.

items.text: A traveller buys euros before flying to Europe
A traveller sells leftover pounds after a trip
A tourist buys dollars for a holiday
The bank buys back unused dollars
A student buys yen before studying abroad
A returning tourist exchanges foreign cash for rand

questions.memo: Buying foreign currency = bank selling rate. Selling leftover foreign currency back = bank buying rate.

questions.question: Which rate is usually LESS favourable to the traveller who is obtaining foreign currency?
questions.memo: When buying currency, the traveller pays the higher selling rate, which is less favourable to them than the buying rate.

questions.question: True or false: A traveller who buys foreign currency and then sells it straight back usually gets back slightly less than they paid.
questions.memo: Because of the gap between the selling and buying rates (the bank's margin), they get back a little less.

questions.question: BSR stands for:
questions.memo: BSR is the Bank Selling Rate — the rate at which the bank sells foreign currency.

questions.question: BBR stands for the bank _________ rate.
questions.memo: BBR is the Bank Buying Rate — the rate at which the bank buys foreign currency back.

questions.question: A tourist plans an overseas trip and visits the bank a week early. They will mainly use the:
options: Bank selling rate to buy foreign currency
Bank buying rate to buy foreign currency
questions.expected: Bank selling rate to buy foreign currency
questions.memo: Buying foreign currency before the trip means the bank sells to them at the bank selling rate.

questions.question: True or false: When you return home and change foreign cash back to rand, the bank buying rate applies.
questions.memo: Changing foreign cash back to rand means the bank buys it from you, using the bank buying rate.

questions.question: Which phrase best helps you remember the rates?
options: Read it from the bank's side: it SELLS to you (BSR) or BUYS from you (BBR)
Read it from the tourist's side only
Both rates are always the same number
The rates depend on the weather
questions.expected: Read it from the bank's side: it SELLS to you (BSR) or BUYS from you (BBR)
questions.memo: Always view the rate from the bank: selling rate when it sells you currency, buying rate when it buys from you.

questions.question: A bureau de change shows two rates for the US dollar. The HIGHER rate (more rand per dollar) is most likely the:
options: Bank selling rate (what you pay to buy dollars)
Bank buying rate (what you get when selling dollars)
questions.expected: Bank selling rate (what you pay to buy dollars)
questions.memo: The selling rate is higher (you pay more rand per dollar); the buying rate is lower (you get less rand per dollar).

questions.question: The gap between the bank selling rate and bank buying rate represents the bank's _________.
questions.memo: The difference between the two rates is the bank's margin, how it profits from exchanging currency.

questions.question: True or false: Knowing the difference between BSR and BBR helps a traveller understand why they pay more to buy currency than they get back when selling it.
questions.memo: The BSR/BBR difference explains why buying currency costs more than what you receive when selling it back.

questions.question: A returning tourist has unused euros. To turn them back into rand, the bank applies the:
questions.memo: The bank buys the euros from the tourist, so the bank buying rate applies.

questions.question: Which statement correctly matches the action to the rate?
options: Buying foreign currency → BSR; selling it back → BBR
Buying foreign currency → BBR; selling it back → BSR
Both actions use the same rate
questions.expected: Buying foreign currency → BSR; selling it back → BBR
questions.memo: Buying uses the bank selling rate; selling back uses the bank buying rate.

questions.question: Why should a traveller only exchange the foreign cash they expect to need?
options: Selling leftover currency back loses a little to the bank's margin
Because foreign cash cannot be used at all
Because the time zone changes the cash
Because banks never buy back currency
questions.expected: Selling leftover currency back loses a little to the bank's margin
questions.memo: Each exchange loses a little to the bank's margin, so changing back unused currency costs the traveller money.

TOUR.G12.T3.EXRATE.A1.title: Effect of exchange-rate fluctuations on tourism
TOUR.G12.T3.EXRATE.A1.description: How rises and falls in the exchange rate affect both inbound and outbound tourism; how a weak or strong rand changes the travel patterns of South Africans heading to developing and developed countries; and the impact of fluctuations on the affordability of destinations.
TOUR.G12.T3.EXRATE.A1.strand: Term 3 — World Heritage Sites, foreign exchange & international travel
TOUR.G12.T3.EXRATE.A1.recovery_strategy: Trace the chain: a weaker rand makes SA CHEAPER for inbound tourists (more arrivals) and makes overseas trips DEARER for South Africans (fewer outbound). A stronger rand reverses both. Follow the money to the tourist's wallet.

questions.question: What is an exchange rate?
options: The value of one currency compared with another
The number of tourists in a country
The star grading of a hotel
questions.expected: The value of one currency compared with another
questions.memo: An exchange rate tells you how much one currency is worth in terms of another, such as the rand against the dollar.

questions.question: When exchange rates 'fluctuate', it means they:
questions.memo: Fluctuating exchange rates rise and fall over time, changing the cost of travel.

questions.question: If the rand weakens, inbound foreign tourism to South Africa is likely to:
options: Increase, because South Africa becomes cheaper for foreigners
Decrease, because South Africa becomes more expensive
questions.expected: Increase, because South Africa becomes cheaper for foreigners
questions.memo: A weaker rand makes South Africa cheaper for foreigners, encouraging more inbound tourists.

questions.question: If the rand strengthens, overseas travel for South Africans becomes _________.
questions.memo: A stronger rand buys more foreign currency, so overseas trips become cheaper for South Africans.

questions.question: True or false: A weaker rand tends to reduce the number of South Africans travelling overseas.
questions.memo: A weaker rand makes overseas trips more expensive, so fewer South Africans travel abroad.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis by choosing the strong supporting points.
questions.thesis: Exchange-rate changes strongly affect tourists' travel decisions.

pool.text: A weaker rand makes South Africa cheaper, drawing more inbound tourists
A stronger rand makes overseas trips cheaper for South Africans, encouraging outbound travel
When trips become too costly, tourists change destinations or stay home
Some tourists prefer window seats on planes
Hotels often have swimming pools

questions.memo: The strong points trace exchange-rate changes to where and whether tourists travel. The red herrings are unrelated to exchange rates.

questions.question: A strong rand can hurt South Africa's inbound tourism because:
options: It makes the country more expensive for foreign visitors
It makes the country cheaper for foreign visitors
questions.expected: It makes the country more expensive for foreign visitors
questions.memo: A strong rand means foreigners get fewer rands, making South Africa pricier and possibly reducing inbound arrivals.

questions.question: Sort each outcome under whether it follows a WEAK rand or a STRONG rand.

items.text: More foreign tourists visit South Africa
South Africans find overseas trips cheaper
Overseas holidays cost South Africans more
South Africa becomes pricier for foreigners
More South Africans choose to holiday locally

questions.memo: A weak rand boosts inbound tourism and local travel; a strong rand boosts outbound travel but raises prices for foreigners.

questions.question: True or false: Exchange-rate fluctuations affect both inbound and outbound tourism.
questions.memo: Changes in the exchange rate affect both foreigners coming in and South Africans going out.

questions.question: When the rand weakens sharply, many South Africans choose to:
options: Travel overseas far more than before
Stop all travel of any kind
Pay no attention to the cost
questions.memo: A weaker rand makes overseas travel costly, so South Africans tend to switch to cheaper domestic travel.

questions.question: When the rand is weak, a South African might choose a holiday in a nearby _________ country rather than an expensive long-haul trip.
questions.memo: A weak rand pushes travellers towards cheaper, often nearby developing destinations rather than costly developed ones.

questions.question: Why is a stable exchange rate helpful for the tourism industry?
options: Businesses and tourists can plan and price trips with more certainty
It removes the need for any marketing
questions.expected: Businesses and tourists can plan and price trips with more certainty
questions.memo: A stable rate makes prices predictable, helping tourists budget and businesses plan.

questions.question: True or false: A sudden strengthening of the rand could discourage some foreign tourists from visiting South Africa.
questions.memo: A stronger rand raises prices for foreigners, which can discourage some from visiting.

questions.question: A British tourist notices their pounds buy far more in South Africa than a year ago. This is because the rand has:
questions.memo: If pounds buy more rands and goods, the rand has weakened against the pound, making the trip cheaper.

questions.question: How might a tour operator respond to a weak rand to attract foreign tourists?
options: Market South Africa as an affordable, good-value destination
Raise prices far above other countries
questions.expected: Market South Africa as an affordable, good-value destination
questions.memo: When the rand is weak, operators can market South Africa as excellent value to draw foreign visitors.

questions.question: A South African family cancels a planned trip to Europe after the rand drops sharply. This shows exchange rates affecting:
questions.memo: South Africans changing or cancelling overseas plans because of the rate is an effect on outbound tourism.

questions.question: True or false: Exchange-rate changes can influence which destinations tourists choose.
questions.memo: Because rates change how affordable a destination is, they can shift where tourists decide to go.

questions.question: A weak rand can be a mixed blessing because it:
options: Helps inbound tourism but makes outbound travel and imports more expensive
Helps everyone equally with no downside
questions.expected: Helps inbound tourism but makes outbound travel and imports more expensive
questions.memo: A weak rand boosts inbound tourism but raises the cost of outbound travel and imported goods — a mixed effect.

questions.question: Which traveller benefits MOST from a strong rand?
options: A South African planning an overseas holiday
A foreign tourist visiting South Africa
questions.expected: A South African planning an overseas holiday
questions.memo: A strong rand gives South Africans more buying power abroad, so outbound travellers benefit most.

questions.question: Which statement best summarises the effect of exchange rates on tourism?
options: A weak rand favours inbound tourism; a strong rand favours outbound tourism
Exchange rates have no effect on tourism
A weak rand favours outbound tourism; a strong rand favours inbound tourism
Only domestic tourism is affected by exchange rates
questions.expected: A weak rand favours inbound tourism; a strong rand favours outbound tourism
questions.memo: A weak rand draws foreigners in (inbound); a strong rand lets South Africans travel out (outbound) more cheaply.

TOUR.G12.T3.PAYMENT.A1.title: Forms of payment when travelling internationally
TOUR.G12.T3.PAYMENT.A1.description: Forms of payment for international travel — electronic fund transfers (EFT), telegraphic/SWIFT transfers, bank drafts, internet payments, foreign bank notes (cash), credit cards, traveller's cheques and preloaded foreign-currency cards — and the advantages and disadvantages of each.
TOUR.G12.T3.PAYMENT.A1.strand: Term 3 — World Heritage Sites, foreign exchange & international travel
TOUR.G12.T3.PAYMENT.A1.recovery_strategy: Weigh each form on safety, convenience and cost. Cash is convenient but risky if lost or stolen; cards and preloaded cards are safer and can be cancelled; traveller's cheques are replaceable but less widely accepted today.

questions.question: Which of these is a form of payment a traveller can use internationally?
questions.memo: A credit card is a widely accepted form of payment for international travel.

questions.question: What is a key DISADVANTAGE of carrying large amounts of cash while travelling?
options: If it is lost or stolen, it usually cannot be replaced
It cannot be spent on small items
questions.expected: If it is lost or stolen, it usually cannot be replaced
questions.memo: Cash is convenient but risky: lost or stolen cash is generally gone for good.

questions.question: An advantage of paying by credit card abroad is that:
options: It is widely accepted and can be cancelled if lost or stolen
It can never be used online
It must always be paid in coins
It only works in South Africa
questions.expected: It is widely accepted and can be cancelled if lost or stolen
questions.memo: Credit cards are widely accepted and can be cancelled if lost or stolen, making them safer than cash.

questions.question: Moving money electronically from one bank account to another is called an electronic fund _________ (EFT).
questions.memo: An electronic fund transfer (EFT) moves money electronically between bank accounts.

questions.question: True or false: A preloaded foreign-currency card (such as a travel card) can be cancelled if lost, making it safer than cash.
questions.memo: A preloaded travel card can be blocked or cancelled if lost or stolen, making it safer than carrying cash.

questions.question: A traveller loads a set amount of foreign currency onto a card before the trip. This is a:
questions.memo: A preloaded travel card holds a set amount of foreign currency loaded before travelling.

questions.question: Sort each payment form under whether it is mainly CASH-BASED or ELECTRONIC/CARD-BASED.

items.text: Coins and notes in a wallet

questions.memo: Bank notes and coins are cash; credit cards, EFTs, travel cards and internet payments are electronic or card-based.

questions.question: An international electronic transfer between banks, often called a SWIFT transfer, is also known as a _________ transfer.
questions.memo: A telegraphic (SWIFT) transfer moves money electronically between banks across borders.

questions.question: True or false: Traveller's cheques can usually be replaced if lost or stolen.
questions.memo: A key advantage of traveller's cheques is that they can be replaced if lost or stolen, unlike cash.

questions.question: A disadvantage of traveller's cheques today is that:
options: They are accepted in fewer places than before
They cannot be replaced if lost
questions.expected: They are accepted in fewer places than before
questions.memo: Traveller's cheques are less widely accepted now that cards are common, which is a disadvantage.

questions.question: Paying for a hotel by entering card details on the hotel's secure website is an example of an:
questions.memo: Entering card details online to pay is an internet payment, a common electronic form of payment.

questions.question: Which is an ADVANTAGE of carrying some cash when travelling?
options: It is handy for small purchases, tips and places that do not take cards
It can be cancelled if lost
It earns interest while you travel
questions.expected: It is handy for small purchases, tips and places that do not take cards
questions.memo: Cash is convenient for small payments, tips and places that do not accept cards.

questions.question: Common credit card brands accepted internationally include Visa, MasterCard and:
questions.memo: Visa, MasterCard, American Express and Diners Club are widely accepted international card brands.

questions.question: True or false: It is wise for a traveller to use more than one form of payment in case one is lost or not accepted.
questions.memo: Carrying a mix (some cash plus a card) is safer, so a traveller is not stranded if one fails or is lost.

questions.question: A written order from a bank to pay a set sum, sometimes used for larger international payments, is a bank _________.
questions.memo: A bank draft is a guaranteed written order from a bank to pay a set amount, used for some larger payments.

questions.question: Why might a traveller prefer a card over carrying all their money as cash?
options: A card is safer because it can be stopped if lost or stolen
A card cannot be used to buy anything
Cash is impossible to spend abroad
A card changes the time zone
questions.expected: A card is safer because it can be stopped if lost or stolen
questions.memo: Cards are safer than cash because they can be cancelled or stopped if lost or stolen.

questions.question: Which payment form is BEST for leaving a small tip for a waiter abroad?
questions.memo: Cash is the most practical way to leave a small tip; drafts and transfers are for larger, formal payments.

questions.question: True or false: Internet and card payments can sometimes carry fees or risks such as online fraud.
questions.memo: Electronic payments can carry transaction fees and some risk of online fraud, which is a disadvantage to weigh up.

questions.question: Which pairing of payment form and feature is CORRECT?
options: Cash — convenient but risky if lost; card — safer and can be cancelled
Cash — can always be cancelled; card — impossible to replace
Cash — only for online use; card — only for tips
Both cash and card cannot be used abroad
questions.expected: Cash — convenient but risky if lost; card — safer and can be cancelled
questions.memo: Cash is convenient but risky; cards are safer and can be cancelled if lost — a correct comparison.

questions.question: When choosing a form of payment for an overseas trip, a traveller should mainly weigh:
options: Safety, convenience and cost (fees) of each option
The colour of the bank notes
The star grading of the bank
The time zone of the bank
questions.expected: Safety, convenience and cost (fees) of each option
questions.memo: The main factors are how safe, convenient and costly each payment form is for the trip.

TOUR.G12.T3.GLOBALEVENTS.A1.title: Global events & unforeseen occurrences
TOUR.G12.T3.GLOBALEVENTS.A1.description: The concept of a global event (e.g. the FIFA World Cup, Olympic Games); the positive and negative impact of hosting on international and domestic tourism and on the host economy (infrastructure, investment, foreign-exchange income, the multiplier effect); and unforeseen occurrences of international significance (natural disasters, disease, recession, political unrest, terrorism) and their impact on tourism.
TOUR.G12.T3.GLOBALEVENTS.A1.strand: Term 3 — World Heritage Sites, foreign exchange & international travel
TOUR.G12.T3.GLOBALEVENTS.A1.recovery_strategy: A GLOBAL EVENT is planned and hosted on purpose (World Cup, Olympics) and usually boosts tourism; an UNFORESEEN OCCURRENCE is sudden and unwanted (tsunami, pandemic, unrest) and usually harms it. Ask: planned or unexpected?

questions.question: What is a 'global event' in tourism?
options: A large event of international importance that a country hosts, such as the FIFA World Cup
A small local school sports day
questions.expected: A large event of international importance that a country hosts, such as the FIFA World Cup
questions.memo: A global event is a large, internationally important event a country hosts, like the FIFA World Cup or Olympic Games.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of a global SPORTING event?
options: A general election in one town
questions.memo: The Olympic Games is a planned global sporting event; the others are not hosted sporting events.

questions.question: What is an 'unforeseen occurrence' of international significance?
options: A sudden, unexpected event such as a natural disaster, disease outbreak or unrest
questions.expected: A sudden, unexpected event such as a natural disaster, disease outbreak or unrest
questions.memo: An unforeseen occurrence is sudden and unexpected — a disaster, disease, recession or unrest — not something planned.

questions.question: Hosting a successful global event can _________ a country's international tourism by raising its profile.
questions.memo: A well-run global event raises a country's profile and can boost its international tourism.

questions.question: True or false: South Africa hosted the 2010 FIFA World Cup, a major global event.
questions.memo: South Africa hosted the 2010 FIFA World Cup, which raised its international profile as a tourism destination.

questions.question: Which is a POSITIVE impact of hosting a global event for the host country?
options: New infrastructure, investment and foreign-exchange income
questions.expected: New infrastructure, investment and foreign-exchange income
questions.memo: Hosting can bring improved infrastructure, investment and foreign-exchange income — positive impacts.

questions.question: Sort each example under whether it is a planned GLOBAL EVENT or an UNFORESEEN OCCURRENCE.
questions.memo: Planned global events (World Cup, Olympics, Tour de France) are hosted on purpose; earthquakes, disease and recession are unforeseen occurrences.

questions.question: When tourist spending circulates through the economy after a big event, supporting many businesses, this is the _________ effect.
questions.memo: The multiplier effect describes how spending from an event spreads through the economy, supporting many businesses.

questions.question: Which is a possible NEGATIVE impact of hosting a global event?
options: Very high costs to build stadiums and infrastructure
questions.expected: Very high costs to build stadiums and infrastructure
questions.memo: Hosting can be very expensive; the high cost of stadiums and infrastructure is a negative impact.

questions.question: How can a disease outbreak affect international tourism in the affected country?
options: Tourists may cancel trips, reducing arrivals and income
It has no effect on tourism
questions.expected: Tourists may cancel trips, reducing arrivals and income
questions.memo: An unforeseen occurrence like a disease outbreak can frighten tourists away, cutting arrivals and tourism income.

questions.question: True or false: Hosting a global event can increase domestic tourism in the host country as locals travel to attend.
questions.memo: Locals travelling to attend a global event boosts domestic tourism in the host country.

questions.question: Political unrest or terrorism in a country is most likely to:
options: Discourage tourists and reduce international arrivals
Encourage far more tourists to visit
Have no effect on tourism at all
questions.expected: Discourage tourists and reduce international arrivals
questions.memo: Unrest and terrorism make tourists feel unsafe, reducing international arrivals to the affected country.

questions.question: A natural disaster such as a _________ is an example of an unforeseen occurrence that can harm tourism.
questions.memo: A tsunami is a natural disaster — an unforeseen occurrence that can damage a destination's tourism.

questions.question: Why is improved infrastructure (roads, airports, stadiums) a lasting benefit of hosting a global event?
options: It can keep serving tourists and locals long after the event
It is removed immediately after the event
It has no use after the event
questions.expected: It can keep serving tourists and locals long after the event
questions.memo: Infrastructure built for an event continues to benefit tourism and the public for years afterwards.

questions.question: True or false: A global recession is a planned global event that countries choose to host.
questions.memo: A global recession is an unforeseen occurrence, not a planned event a country hosts.

questions.question: Foreign visitors who come for a global event and spend money bring in valuable:
questions.memo: International visitors spending foreign currency provide foreign-exchange income for the host country.

questions.question: How can a country reduce the negative tourism impact of an unforeseen occurrence?
options: Reassure tourists with clear safety information and recovery plans
questions.expected: Reassure tourists with clear safety information and recovery plans
questions.memo: Clear, honest safety communication and recovery efforts help rebuild tourist confidence after an unforeseen occurrence.

questions.question: True or false: The positive and negative impacts of a global event should both be weighed before a country decides to host it.
questions.memo: Both benefits (profile, investment) and costs (expense, disruption) should be considered before hosting.

questions.question: Which best describes the impact of an unforeseen occurrence on the economy of an affected country?
options: It can reduce tourism income and damage businesses that rely on visitors
questions.expected: It can reduce tourism income and damage businesses that rely on visitors
questions.memo: Fewer tourists after an unforeseen occurrence means less income for tourism businesses and the wider economy.

questions.question: Which statement correctly contrasts the two concepts?
options: A global event is planned and usually helps tourism; an unforeseen occurrence is sudden and usually harms it
Both are planned and both help tourism
A global event harms tourism; an unforeseen occurrence helps it
questions.expected: A global event is planned and usually helps tourism; an unforeseen occurrence is sudden and usually harms it
questions.memo: Global events are planned and tend to boost tourism; unforeseen occurrences are sudden and tend to harm it.

TOUR.G12.T3.MARKETSHARE.A1.title: Foreign market share & inbound statistics
TOUR.G12.T3.MARKETSHARE.A1.description: Interpreting inbound international tourism statistics — foreign arrivals to South Africa (land and air), how arrivals determine foreign market share, the most-visited provinces, length of stay, average expenditure per tourist and activities undertaken — using sources such as StatsSA and South African Tourism reports.
TOUR.G12.T3.MARKETSHARE.A1.strand: Term 3 — World Heritage Sites, foreign exchange & international travel
TOUR.G12.T3.MARKETSHARE.A1.recovery_strategy: Read the table heading and units before answering. Market SHARE is a country's portion of total arrivals (a percentage of the whole); raw arrivals is a count. Match each question to the correct column.

questions.question: What does 'foreign market share' mean for South African tourism?
options: The portion of total foreign arrivals that come from a particular market or country
The number of South Africans who travel abroad
The price of a foreign airline ticket
The star grading of a hotel
questions.expected: The portion of total foreign arrivals that come from a particular market or country
questions.memo: Foreign market share is the share (portion) of total foreign arrivals coming from a given country or market.

questions.question: Foreign arrivals to South Africa are counted through which two main travel markets?
questions.memo: Foreign arrival statistics are gathered mainly from the land and air travel markets.

questions.question: Which organisation is a reliable SOURCE of inbound tourism statistics for South Africa?
questions.memo: StatsSA and South African Tourism are official sources of inbound tourism statistics.

questions.question: The average amount each tourist spends during their visit is called the average _________ per tourist.
questions.memo: Average expenditure per tourist is the typical amount each visitor spends, a key statistic.

questions.question: True or false: Statistics on the most-visited provinces help show where foreign tourists go in South Africa.
questions.memo: Most-visited-province statistics reveal which parts of South Africa foreign tourists favour.

questions.question: If 100 000 foreign tourists arrive and 25 000 are from the United Kingdom, the UK's market share is:
questions.memo: 25 000 out of 100 000 is one quarter, or 25% — the UK's market share of arrivals.

questions.question: Why is 'length of stay' a useful statistic?
options: Longer stays usually mean more spending in the country
questions.expected: Longer stays usually mean more spending in the country
questions.memo: The longer tourists stay, the more they tend to spend, so length of stay matters for tourism income.

questions.question: Compare these two short reports, then judge each statement.

source_a.text: Foreign air arrivals to South Africa rose by 12% this year, with Gauteng the most-visited province and an average stay of 9 nights.

source_b.text: Our airline added three new international routes this year and painted its planes in bright new colours for the summer season.

statements.text: Gives official inbound tourism statistics useful for market share
Is mainly marketing or promotional content
Mentions air travel in some way
Reports the average daily exchange rate

questions.memo: Source A is official statistics useful for market share; Source B is promotional. Both mention air travel; neither reports an exchange rate.

questions.question: Which statistic tells you what foreign tourists DID while visiting South Africa?
options: Activities undertaken whilst in the country
questions.expected: Activities undertaken whilst in the country
questions.memo: Statistics on activities undertaken show what tourists did, such as safaris, beaches or city tours.

questions.question: A rise in foreign arrivals usually leads to a _________ in foreign-exchange income for the country.
questions.memo: More foreign arrivals generally means more foreign currency spent, raising foreign-exchange income.

questions.question: True or false: Market share is shown as a portion (or percentage) of the total arrivals, not just a raw number.
questions.memo: Market share is a portion or percentage of the whole, while raw arrivals is simply a count.

questions.question: Before answering a question from a statistics table, you should first:
options: Read the column headings and units carefully
questions.expected: Read the column headings and units carefully
questions.memo: Reading the headings and units first prevents confusing, say, length of stay with number of arrivals.

questions.question: If a country's share of arrivals grows from 10% to 15%, its market share has:
questions.memo: Going from 10% to 15% is a rise, so that market's share has increased.

questions.question: Why do tourism authorities study which provinces foreign tourists visit most?
options: To plan marketing and services where demand is highest or lowest
questions.expected: To plan marketing and services where demand is highest or lowest
questions.memo: Knowing where tourists go helps authorities plan marketing and improve services in the right places.

questions.question: Statistics showing how many foreign tourists arrived by road fall under the _________ travel market.
questions.memo: Arrivals by road are part of the land travel market; arrivals by plane are the air market.

questions.question: True or false: Comparing this year's arrival statistics with last year's shows whether tourism is growing.
questions.memo: Comparing arrivals across years reveals whether inbound tourism is growing, steady or shrinking.

questions.question: A table shows 'average expenditure per tourist = R12 000'. This means each tourist on average:
options: Spent about R12 000 during their visit
Paid R12 000 in airport tax only
questions.expected: Spent about R12 000 during their visit
questions.memo: Average expenditure per tourist of R12 000 means each visitor spent roughly that amount in total.

questions.question: Why is inbound tourism data important for marketing South Africa?
options: It shows which markets to target and how to attract more visitors
It decides the country's time zone
It replaces the need for attractions
It sets the price of fuel
questions.expected: It shows which markets to target and how to attract more visitors
questions.memo: Knowing where tourists come from and what they do helps target marketing to grow arrivals.

questions.question: Which is the difference between 'raw arrivals' and 'market share'?
options: Raw arrivals is a count; market share is that count as a portion of the total
They mean exactly the same thing
Market share is always a smaller count than raw arrivals
Raw arrivals is a percentage; market share is a count
questions.expected: Raw arrivals is a count; market share is that count as a portion of the total
questions.memo: Raw arrivals is simply how many came; market share expresses that as a portion (percentage) of all arrivals.

questions.question: True or false: Travel journals, in-flight magazines and provincial tourism authorities can also provide useful tourism information.
questions.memo: Besides StatsSA and SA Tourism, travel journals, magazines and provincial authorities also provide tourism information.

TOUR.G12.T4.PILLARS.A1.title: The three pillars & responsible tourists
TOUR.G12.T4.PILLARS.A1.description: The three pillars of sustainable tourism (people, profit, planet) and the triple bottom-line approach; good environmental practices (resource, waste and pollution management; indigenous flora; control of alien plants); the responsible role of business (ownership, employment, local procurement); social effects and corporate social investment (CSI); and what makes a responsible tourist.
TOUR.G12.T4.PILLARS.A1.strand: Term 4 — Responsible tourism, customer satisfaction & marketing SA
TOUR.G12.T4.PILLARS.A1.recovery_strategy: Match each action to its pillar: PLANET = the environment (energy, water, waste, wildlife); PEOPLE = communities and culture (jobs, CSI, respect); PROFIT = the business running responsibly and staying viable. Ask which the action mainly protects.

questions.question: What are the three pillars of sustainable tourism?
questions.memo: The three pillars of sustainable tourism are people (social), profit (economic) and planet (environmental).

questions.question: The 'planet' pillar of sustainable tourism is mainly about:
questions.memo: The planet pillar focuses on protecting the environment — energy, water, waste and nature.

questions.question: Reducing, re-using and recycling waste at a lodge is an example of caring for which pillar?
questions.memo: Managing waste through reduce, re-use and recycle protects the environment — the planet pillar.

questions.question: The 'people' pillar considers the effects of tourism on local communities, culture and _________.
questions.memo: The people (social) pillar looks at tourism's effects on communities, culture and heritage.

questions.question: True or false: The three-pillar approach is also called the 'triple bottom line'.
questions.memo: The triple bottom line is the approach that balances all three pillars: people, profit and planet.

questions.question: A tourism business employing local people and buying local goods is acting on which pillar?
options: Profit (economy), benefiting the local economy responsibly
questions.expected: Profit (economy), benefiting the local economy responsibly
questions.memo: Local employment and procurement are part of the profit (economic) pillar, helping the local economy responsibly.

questions.question: Sort each action under the pillar it mainly supports.

items.text: Employing people from the local community

questions.memo: Planet = environment (water, energy, recycling); people = community and culture (CSI, respect); profit = responsible economy (local jobs and supplies).

questions.question: Financial or non-financial support a tourism company gives to community projects is called corporate social _________ (CSI).
questions.memo: Corporate social investment (CSI) is support tourism companies give to community projects in health, sport, education or youth.

questions.question: True or false: Controlling alien invasive plants and promoting indigenous flora supports the planet pillar.
questions.memo: Promoting indigenous plants and removing invasive aliens protects the environment — the planet pillar.

questions.question: What makes someone a 'responsible tourist'?
options: They respect the environment, local culture and community
They ignore local customs and litter freely
They only care about the cheapest option
questions.expected: They respect the environment, local culture and community
questions.memo: A responsible tourist behaves in ways that respect the environment, culture and people of the place they visit.

questions.question: A hotel installs solar panels and low-flow taps. This mainly supports the _________ pillar.
questions.memo: Saving energy and water through solar panels and low-flow taps protects the environment — the planet pillar.

questions.question: Why must a sustainable tourism business still make a profit?
options: It must stay financially viable to keep operating and supporting people and the planet
Profit is not important at all
So it can ignore the community
questions.expected: It must stay financially viable to keep operating and supporting people and the planet
questions.memo: A business must remain viable (profitable) to keep running and continue benefiting people and the environment.

questions.question: True or false: Sustainable tourism tries to balance all three pillars rather than focusing on only one.
questions.memo: Sustainable tourism balances people, profit and planet together, not just one of them.

questions.question: A negative effect of tourism on local communities (the people pillar) could be:
options: Overcrowding and rising prices that affect residents
questions.expected: Overcrowding and rising prices that affect residents
questions.memo: Tourism can have negative social effects too, such as overcrowding and higher prices for residents.

questions.question: Using energy and water carefully so future generations can also enjoy resources is called responsible _________ management.
questions.memo: Resource management (energy and water) is a good environmental practice under the planet pillar.

questions.question: Which is an example of the PROFIT pillar being practised responsibly?
options: A lodge buys food from nearby farmers and hires local staff
A lodge dumps waste into the river
A lodge ignores the local community
A lodge wastes water and energy
questions.expected: A lodge buys food from nearby farmers and hires local staff
questions.memo: Procuring local goods and employing local people keeps money in the community — responsible profit.

questions.question: True or false: A responsible tourist might choose accommodation that recycles, saves water and supports the local community.
questions.memo: Responsible tourists support businesses that care for the environment and community, reflecting all three pillars.

questions.question: Litter control and pollution control at an attraction are good _________ practices.
questions.memo: Litter and pollution control are good environmental practices supporting the planet pillar.

questions.question: Which choice shows all three pillars working together?
options: A profitable lodge that saves water, recycles and employs and trains local people
A lodge that only chases profit and pollutes
A lodge that ignores both staff and the environment
A lodge that wastes resources but supports the community
questions.expected: A profitable lodge that saves water, recycles and employs and trains local people
questions.memo: Balancing profit (viable business), planet (saving water, recycling) and people (local jobs and training) reflects all three pillars.

questions.question: The main idea of the triple bottom line is that a tourism business should:
options: Care for people and the planet while remaining profitable
Ignore the environment to save money
questions.expected: Care for people and the planet while remaining profitable
questions.memo: The triple bottom line means succeeding on people, profit and planet together, not profit alone.

TOUR.G12.T4.TOURISTCODE.A1.title: Codes of conduct & demand for responsible tourism
TOUR.G12.T4.TOURISTCODE.A1.description: Codes of conduct for tourist behaviour (social, economic and environmental); how a destination can attract responsible, conscious tourists; the growing demand for responsible tourism; and the role of Fair Trade Tourism South Africa (FTTSA) in encouraging responsible and sustainable practices.
TOUR.G12.T4.TOURISTCODE.A1.strand: Term 4 — Responsible tourism, customer satisfaction & marketing SA
TOUR.G12.T4.TOURISTCODE.A1.recovery_strategy: Sort responsible behaviour by the pillar it serves: SOCIAL = respect people and culture; ECONOMIC = support local business and fair pay; ENVIRONMENTAL = protect nature and reduce waste. FTTSA certifies businesses meeting these standards.

questions.question: What is a code of conduct for tourist behaviour?
options: A set of guidelines on how tourists should behave responsibly
A map of world time zones
questions.expected: A set of guidelines on how tourists should behave responsibly
questions.memo: A code of conduct for tourists guides how they should behave responsibly towards people, the economy and the environment.

questions.question: Codes of conduct for tourist behaviour usually cover social, economic and _________ responsibilities.
questions.memo: Tourist codes of conduct cover social, economic and environmental behaviour — matching the three pillars.

questions.question: Which is an example of ENVIRONMENTALLY responsible tourist behaviour?
options: Taking all litter away and staying on marked trails
questions.expected: Taking all litter away and staying on marked trails
questions.memo: Removing litter and staying on trails protects the environment — environmentally responsible behaviour.

questions.question: Buying local crafts and paying fair prices is an example of which kind of responsible behaviour?
questions.memo: Supporting local business and fair pay is economically responsible behaviour, helping the local economy.

questions.question: Respecting local customs, dress and traditions is an example of _________ responsible behaviour.
questions.memo: Respecting local people, customs and culture is socially responsible tourist behaviour.

questions.question: True or false: There is growing demand among tourists for responsible and sustainable travel options.
questions.memo: More tourists now seek responsible, sustainable options, increasing demand for responsible tourism.

questions.question: Build the strongest argument for this thesis by choosing the strong supporting points.
questions.thesis: Tourist codes of conduct help make tourism more sustainable.

pool.text: They guide tourists to protect the environment, such as not littering or disturbing wildlife
They encourage tourists to respect local culture and communities
They promote spending that supports the local economy fairly
They tell tourists which airline seats recline furthest
They list the colours of foreign bank notes

questions.memo: The strong points link the code to protecting the environment, respecting people and supporting the local economy. The red herrings are irrelevant.

questions.question: Sort each tourist behaviour under the type of responsibility it shows.

items.text: Buying from local traders at fair prices
Not littering in a nature reserve
Learning a few words of the local language

questions.memo: Social = respecting people and culture; economic = supporting local business and fair pay; environmental = protecting nature and resources.

questions.question: How can a destination attract environmentally conscious tourists?
options: By offering genuine eco-friendly, responsible tourism options
By polluting more to cut prices
questions.expected: By offering genuine eco-friendly, responsible tourism options
questions.memo: Destinations attract conscious tourists by genuinely offering responsible, eco-friendly experiences.

questions.question: Which organisation encourages responsible and sustainable tourism practices in South Africa?
options: The Department of Home Affairs only
questions.memo: FTTSA promotes and certifies responsible and sustainable (fair trade) tourism practices in South Africa.

questions.question: FTTSA mainly works to certify tourism businesses that practise _________ and sustainable tourism.
questions.memo: FTTSA certifies businesses that practise responsible and sustainable, fair-trade tourism.

questions.question: Which is an example of IRRESPONSIBLE tourist behaviour?
options: Carving your name into an ancient monument
questions.expected: Carving your name into an ancient monument
questions.memo: Damaging a monument is irresponsible; the other options respect heritage, the environment and the economy.

questions.question: True or false: Following a tourist code of conduct can help protect attractions for future visitors.
questions.memo: Responsible behaviour protects attractions and the environment so future visitors can enjoy them too.

questions.question: Why is the demand for responsible tourism important for tourism businesses?
options: Businesses that meet it can attract more customers and stay competitive
It has no effect on business
It only matters to tourists, not businesses
questions.expected: Businesses that meet it can attract more customers and stay competitive
questions.memo: As demand grows, businesses offering responsible options attract more customers and stay competitive.

questions.question: Not disturbing wildlife and keeping a respectful distance shows _________ responsibility.
questions.memo: Protecting wildlife by keeping your distance is environmentally responsible behaviour.

questions.question: A tourist hires a local guide and eats at local restaurants. This benefits the destination's:
questions.memo: Spending on local guides and restaurants supports the local economy — economically responsible behaviour.

questions.question: True or false: Case studies of companies using the triple bottom-line approach can teach tourists and businesses about responsible practices.
questions.memo: Studying real companies that balance people, profit and planet shows how responsible tourism works in practice.

questions.question: Which behaviour best matches a SOCIALLY responsible tourist?
options: Asking permission before photographing local people
Bargaining unfairly to underpay a trader
questions.expected: Asking permission before photographing local people
questions.memo: Asking permission shows respect for local people — socially responsible behaviour.

questions.question: Why might a tourist choose an FTTSA-certified business?
options: It shows the business meets fair, responsible and sustainable standards
It guarantees the cheapest possible price
It removes the need for a passport
questions.expected: It shows the business meets fair, responsible and sustainable standards
questions.memo: FTTSA certification signals that a business meets recognised responsible and sustainable standards.

questions.question: Which statement best sums up a tourist code of conduct?
options: It guides tourists to behave responsibly towards people, the economy and the environment
It sets the price of every tour
It only applies to tour guides, not tourists
It decides which currency to use
questions.expected: It guides tourists to behave responsibly towards people, the economy and the environment
questions.memo: A tourist code of conduct guides responsible behaviour across the social, economic and environmental areas.

TOUR.G12.T4.ROLEPLAYERS.A1.title: Role players in responsible & sustainable tourism
TOUR.G12.T4.ROLEPLAYERS.A1.description: The role players who drive responsible and sustainable tourism — government and local authorities, tourism businesses, communities, tourists themselves and organisations such as FTTSA — and how each contributes through policy, practice, behaviour and certification.
TOUR.G12.T4.ROLEPLAYERS.A1.strand: Term 4 — Responsible tourism, customer satisfaction & marketing SA
TOUR.G12.T4.ROLEPLAYERS.A1.recovery_strategy: Match the job to the player: GOVERNMENT makes policy and laws; BUSINESSES run sustainably and create jobs; COMMUNITIES protect heritage and benefit locally; TOURISTS behave responsibly; FTTSA certifies fair-trade operators.

questions.question: Who are the 'role players' in responsible and sustainable tourism?
options: Everyone involved — government, businesses, communities and tourists
questions.expected: Everyone involved — government, businesses, communities and tourists
questions.memo: Role players are all those who shape tourism: government, businesses, communities, tourists and bodies like FTTSA.

questions.question: What is the main role of GOVERNMENT in sustainable tourism?
options: Making policy and laws that guide and protect tourism
